Further examining the characteristics that our classifiers rely on, we find that features such as passive voice, animacy and case strongly correlate with classification decisions, suggesting that mBERT does not encode subjecthood purely syntactically, but that subjecthood embedding is continuous and dependent on semantic and discourse factors, as is proposed in much of the functional linguistics literature. Together, these results provide insight into how grammatical features manifest in contextual embedding spaces, at a level of abstraction not covered by previous work.

papers.title: Steering into New Embedding Spaces: Analyzing Cross-Lingual Alignment Induced by Model Interventions in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the finding experts intervention on cross-lingual alignment in multilingual language models?
papers.core_contribution: Intervening on language expert neurons in mLLMs projects embeddings into a new space with enhanced cross-lingual alignment, leading to improved performance on cross-lingual retrieval tasks.
papers.conclusion: The finding-experts intervention enhances cross-lingual alignment in mLLMs, improving retrieval performance, and is recommended for aligning representations across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The finding experts intervention shifts the embedding space, reducing distances between languages and increasing cross-lingual alignment.
Post-intervention, cross-lingual retrieval accuracy improves by up to 2x in top-1 accuracy.
Within-language similarity is preserved in the new embedding space, as shown by paraphrase retrieval accuracy.
Intervention on random neurons does not yield similar improvements, indicating the importance of targeting expert neurons.
The intervention is most effective when the model has been trained on both the intervention-target and the languages to be aligned.
papers.limitation:
Lack of access to training data and procedures for the models, limiting deeper analysis.
PolyLM-13b behaves as an outlier in the analyses, possibly due to training differences.
Only one intervention method (finding experts) is studied, leaving other approaches for future work.
future_direction: Explore the effect of intervention on alignment in controlled settings with known training data.
Compare different model intervention methods to understand their impact on representation space.
papers.abstract: Aligned representations across languages is a desired property in multilingual large language models (mLLMs), as alignment can improve performance in cross-lingual tasks. Typically alignment requires fine-tuning a model, which is computationally expensive, and sizable language data, which often may not be available. A data-efficient alternative to fine-tuning is model interventions -- a method for manipulating model activations to steer generation into the desired direction. We analyze the effect of a popular intervention (finding experts) on the alignment of cross-lingual representations in mLLMs. We identify the neurons to manipulate for a given language and introspect the embedding space of mLLMs pre- and post-manipulation. We show that modifying the mLLM's activations changes its embedding space such that cross-lingual alignment is enhanced. Further, we show that the changes to the embedding space translate into improved downstream performance on retrieval tasks, with up to 2x improvements in top-1 accuracy on cross-lingual retrieval.

papers.title: Understanding Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer in Multilingual Recurrent Neural Networks.
papers.research_question: Does exposure to a related language (L1) improve implicit syntactic knowledge in a target language (L2) within multilingual neural networks? Do these networks induce a common representation space with shared syntactic categories?
papers.core_contribution: Cross-lingual syntactic transfer in multilingual neural networks is limited and inconsistent, and optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.
papers.conclusion: Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge is limited and dependent on language pairs, and modern multilingual neural networks are still far from acquiring a true interlingua.
papers.key_findings:
Exposing a model to a related language does not always improve grammatical knowledge in the target language; in some cases, it causes negative interference.
Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge (e.g., long-range agreement in nonce sentences) is very limited and strongly dependent on the specific source-target language pair.
Part-of-speech categories are shared to a moderate extent across languages in the models, but dependency categories are not shared at all.
Language relatedness is the most determining factor for both word embedding alignment and part-of-speech transfer.
Scaling from two to nine input languages improves part-of-speech transfer among related languages but worsens it between unrelated languages.
papers.limitation:
Transfer of syntactic knowledge is limited and inconsistent, with negative interference observed in some language pairs (e.g., French to Italian).
Syntactic knowledge transfer within the models is shallow, with dependency categories not shared across languages.
papers.abstract: It is now established that modern neural language models can be successfully trained on multiple languages simultaneously without changes to the underlying architecture. But what kind of knowledge is really shared among languages within these models? Does multilingual training mostly lead to an alignment of the lexical representation spaces or does it also enable the sharing of purely grammatical knowledge? In this paper we dissect different forms of cross-lingual transfer and look for its most determining factors, using a variety of models and probing tasks. We find that exposing our LMs to a related language does not always increase grammatical knowledge in the target language, and that optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs with variations, and reveals that the last token acts as a function vector encoding relation and language, composed in two stages in decoder-only models.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for factual recall, indicating that knowledge evaluation and editing methods need to be adapted for multilingual settings.
papers.key_findings:
The early MLP site for subject enrichment is present in multilingual LLMs, but the late site involves both MLP and attention, unlike English LLMs where only attention dominates.
Subject information flows similarly to monolingual models, but non-subject token flow differs.
In multilingual decoder-only LLMs, both feed-forward and attention sublayers contribute to object extraction, unlike in English autoregressive LLMs where attention modules dominate.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV) encoding both the relation and the output language.
In decoder-only LLMs, the FV is constructed in two distinct phases: first encoding the relation, then incorporating the language.
future_direction: Developing knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition methods tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying how the function vector is altered across languages to understand if models think in English
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Exploring Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation: Mutual Opportunities and Open Challenges
papers.research_question: Can LLMs leverage both their robust capabilities (in English) and their multilingual knowledge (in non-English languages) during inference to further unlock their multilingual potential?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation (X Transplant), a probing framework that transplants latent activations across languages at inference time to unlock multilingual and cultural knowledge in LLMs, revealing underutilized potential.
papers.conclusion: The analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
X Transplant has mutually beneficial effects on multilingual capability and cultural adaptability, especially for low-resource languages and cultures.
Attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge.
The upper-bound performance of X Transplant reveals a significant underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential.
English boosts multilingual capability, while non-English improves cultural adaptability.
papers.abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) often exhibit imbalances in multilingual capabilities and cultural adaptability, largely attributed to their English-centric pre-training data. In this paper, we introduce and investigate a cross-lingual latent transplantation (XTransplant) framework, which aims to further exploit the model's internalized multilingual knowledge during inference and examine its effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs. XTransplant framework enables models to harness the complementary strengths of both English and non-English resources by transplanting latent activations across languages. Through extensive analysis, we empirically demonstrate that XTransplant, a form of cross-lingual interaction, has mutually beneficial effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs, particularly for low-resource languages and cultures. We further reveal that attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge. In addition, we conduct in-depth analysis of XTransplant's stability, effectiveness, and generalizability. By probing the upper bound performance of XTransplant, we expose the considerable underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential-a challenge that remains open. We hope our analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: Do Multilingual Neural Machine Translation Models Contain Language Pair Specific Attention Heads?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual neural machine translation models contain language pair specific attention heads? The paper investigates this by analyzing individual attention heads in a many-to-one NMT model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in a multilingual NMT model, the most important attention heads are largely language-independent, and about 30% of heads can be pruned without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Although rare language-pair specific attention heads exist, the most important heads are language-independent, and around 30% of heads can be pruned without retraining and with almost no loss in BLEU.
papers.key_findings:
The set of most important attention heads is very similar across different language pairs.
It is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important attention heads without greatly hurting translation quality.
For encoder-decoder (cross) attention heads, the coverage metric is a better indicator for pruning importance, while for encoder self-attention heads, the confidence metric is more effective.
Some rare attention heads are language-pair specific, as identified by the exhaustive Sequential Backward Selection (SBS) procedure.
The variance, confidence, and coverage metrics provide a proxy for head importance, but the SBS algorithm yields the best ranking for pruning.
future_direction: Perform pruning at different levels of granularity (beyond single scalar metrics) to identify which parts of the model are more language-specific.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on the analysis of the multilingual representations focus on identifying whether there is an emergence of languageindependent representations, or whether a multilingual model partitions its weights among different languages. While most of such work has been conducted in a "black-box" manner, this paper aims to analyze individual components of a multilingual neural translation (NMT) model. In particular, we look at the encoder self-attention and encoder-decoder attention heads (in a many-to-one NMT model) that are more specific to the translation of a certain language pair than others by (1) employing metrics that quantify some aspects of the attention weights such as "variance" or "confidence", and (2) systematically ranking the importance of attention heads with respect to translation quality. Experimental results show that surprisingly, the set of most important attention heads are very similar across the language pairs and that it is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important heads without hurting the translation quality greatly.

papers.title: Do Large Language Models know who did what to whom?
papers.research_question: Does the central training objective of LLMs—word prediction—result in sentence representations that capture thematic roles (who did what to whom)?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can extract thematic roles from sentences, but this information has a weaker influence on their internal representations compared to human judgments, which are more strongly influenced by thematic roles than syntax.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can extract thematic roles but, relative to humans, this information influences their representations more weakly.
papers.key_findings:
In LLMs, the overall representational similarity of sentence pairs reflected syntactic similarity but not whether their agent and patient assignments were identical vs. reversed.
Human similarity judgments were more influenced by thematic roles than syntax, opposite to LLMs.
Some attention heads robustly captured thematic roles independently of syntax.
There was little evidence that thematic role information was available in any subset of hidden units.
Thematic role information influences LLM representations more weakly than in humans.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are commonly criticized for not understanding language. However, many critiques focus on cognitive abilities that, in humans, are distinct from language processing. Here, we instead study a kind of understanding tightly linked to language: inferring who did what to whom (thematic roles) in a sentence. Does the central training objective of LLMs-word prediction-result in sentence representations that capture thematic roles? In two experiments, we characterized sentence representations in four LLMs. In contrast to human similarity judgments, in LLMs the overall representational similarity of sentence pairs reflected syntactic similarity but not whether their agent and patient assignments were identical vs. reversed. Furthermore, we found little evidence that thematic role information was available in any subset of hidden units. However, some attention heads robustly captured thematic roles, independently of syntax. Therefore, LLMs can extract thematic roles but, relative to humans, this information influences their representations more weakly.

papers.title: Different types of syntactic agreement recruit the same units within large language models
papers.research_question: We investigate whether different syntactic phenomena recruit shared or distinct components in LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that syntactic agreement phenomena recruit overlapping units in large language models, suggesting that agreement forms a functional category, and this pattern holds across languages with overlap correlating with syntactic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that syntactic agreement constitutes a meaningful category within LLMs' representational spaces, with shared units across agreement types and languages, organized by syntactic similarity.
papers.key_findings:
Syntax-responsive units are consistently identified across sentence instances for each syntactic phenomenon and causally support model performance.
Different types of syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor, determiner-noun) recruit overlapping sets of units in English.
The overlap among agreement units is higher than with non-agreement phenomena, indicating agreement as a shared functional category.
This pattern replicates in Russian and Chinese, with agreement units showing cross-lingual overlap.
Cross-lingual unit overlap for subject-verb agreement increases with syntactic similarity across 57 languages.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on top-n% unit localization may overlook more distributed syntactic representations.
Analyses are primarily correlational, though causal involvement is demonstrated via ablation.
Focus on benchmarks comparing grammatical to ungrammatical sentences, which may not capture full grammatical knowledge.
future_direction: Apply the approach to other syntactic phenomena, including infrequent structures, ambiguities, and long-distance dependencies.
Extend experiments to other languages with BLiMP-like benchmarks, such as Dutch or Turkish.
Investigate the relationship between syntax and semantics in model representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reliably distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences, but how grammatical knowledge is represented within the models remains an open question. We investigate whether different syntactic phenomena recruit shared or distinct components in LLMs. Using a functional localization approach inspired by cognitive neuroscience, we identify the LLM units most responsive to 67 English syntactic phenomena in seven open-weight models. These units are consistently recruited across sentences containing the phenomena and causally support the models' syntactic performance. Critically, different types of syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor, determiner-noun) recruit overlapping sets of units, suggesting that agreement constitutes a meaningful functional category for LLMs. This pattern holds in English, Russian, and Chinese; and further, in a cross-lingual analysis of 57 diverse languages, structurally more similar languages share more units for subject-verb agreement. Taken together, these findings reveal that syntactic agreement-a critical marker of syntactic dependencies-constitutes a meaningful category within LLMs' representational spaces.

papers.title: Contributions of Transformer Attention Heads in Multi- and Cross-lingual Tasks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer-based models on cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, and how can important heads be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that pruning a subset of attention heads in multilingual Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-R) generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and introduces a gradient-based method to rank and identify which heads to prune.
papers.conclusion: Pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer models generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and the gradient-based method effectively identifies heads to prune, offering better model interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning attention heads in mBERT and XLM-R generally has positive effects on model performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF).
A gradient-based method can effectively rank attention heads by importance, and pruning the lowest-ranked heads leads to performance improvements.
The important attention heads for a task are shared across languages, as evidenced by high correlation in head rankings across different languages.
Pruning attention heads is beneficial even when training data in the target language is limited, making models more applicable to resource-poor languages.
In multi-source language settings, pruning attention heads also improves performance, and the gradient-based ranking method can be extended to multiple source languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF) and may not generalize to other cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Improving model interpretability in other cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, e.g., XNLI and other passage-level classification tasks.
papers.abstract: Weicheng Ma, Kai Zhang, Renze Lou, Lili Wang, Soroush Vosoughi. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression: From Language-Specific to Shared Neurons
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models achieve cross-lingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, with representations evolving from language-specific to shared cross-lingual abstractions, demonstrated via neuron analysis and manipulation.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, leading to the development of shared concept neurons across languages that encode generalized semantic representations.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models initially form language-specific representations which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.
Language identification probing reveals a shift from uniform capabilities across layers to specialized layer functions, with middle layers becoming more language-agnostic.
Specific neurons emerge as reliable predictors for the same semantic concepts across different languages, showing increasing alignment during training.
Neuron manipulation experiments demonstrate that concept-specific neurons identified from one language can guide semantically coherent text generation in another language once cross-lingual generalization is achieved.
The model's internal representations encode shared conceptual knowledge independent of the original language encoding.
papers.limitation: The number of publicly available training checkpoints for the BLOOM models is limited, restricting the granularity of analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to transfer knowledge across languages, despite being trained without explicit cross-lingual supervision.We analyze the parameter spaces of three MLLMs to study how their representations evolve during pre-training, observing patterns consistent with compression: models initially form language-specific representations, which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.Through probing experiments, we observe a clear transition from uniform language identification capabilities across layers to more specialized layer functions.For deeper analysis, we focus on neurons that encode distinct semantic concepts.By tracing their development during pre-training, we show how they gradually align across languages.Notably, we identify specific neurons that emerge as increasingly reliable predictors for the same concepts across languages.This alignment manifests concretely in generation: once an MLLM exhibits cross-lingual generalization according to our measures, we can select concept-specific neurons identified from, e.g., Spanish text and manipulate them to guide token predictions.Remarkably, rather than generating Spanish text, the model produces semantically coherent English text.This demonstrates that cross-lingually aligned neurons encode generalized semantic representations, independent of the original language encoding.

papers.title: When classifying grammatical role, BERT doesn’t care about word order... except when it matters
papers.research_question: How do BERT and GPT-2 represent grammatical role, especially in non-prototypical sentences where word order is necessary for correct classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that word order is crucial for grammatical role representation in non-prototypical cases, with syntactic information gradually emerging in later layers of BERT and GPT-2, while early layers rely on lexical semantics.
papers.conclusion: Considering non-prototypical instances is crucial for understanding how language models represent syntactic information, as average probing can be misleading.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantics dominates early layer embeddings, while syntactic word order information is acquired in later layers for non-prototypical sentences.
Models can represent meaning based on syntactic word order, overriding lexical cues, as demonstrated with argument-swapped sentences.
Syntactic word order is significant beyond local coherence, as probes fail on locally shuffled sentences for non-prototypical cases.
papers.abstract: Because meaning can often be inferred from lexical semantics alone, word order is often a redundant cue in natural language. For example, the words chopped, chef, and onion are more likely used to convey "The chef chopped the onion," not "The onion chopped the chef." Recent work has shown large language models to be surprisingly word order invariant, but crucially has largely considered natural prototypical inputs, where compositional meaning mostly matches lexical expectations. To overcome this confound, we probe grammatical role representation in English BERT and GPT-2, on instances where lexical expectations are not sufficient, and word order knowledge is necessary for correct classification. Such nonprototypical instances are naturally occurring English sentences with inanimate subjects or animate objects, or sentences where we systematically swap the arguments to make sentences like "The onion chopped the chef". We find that, while early layer embeddings are largely lexical, word order is in fact crucial in defining the later-layer representations of words in semantically non-prototypical positions. Our experiments isolate the effect of word order on the contextualization process, and highlight how models use context in the uncommon, but critical, instances where it matters.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, enabling targeted extraction of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by causal effects on language modeling performance and direct subspace comparisons.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages.
Stable language-neutral axes encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech, and these axes are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
The identified axes (both language-sensitive and language-neutral) are relatively stable across middle layers of the model.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures like spirals, toruses, and curves in the representation space.
future_direction: Investigate how nonlinear structures (e.g., spirals, toruses) arise from and interact with the dot product self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.

Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically, and the extent to which representation spaces can be fully decomposed into orthogonal subspaces encoding different features.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: Cross-neutralising: Probing for joint encoding of linguistic information in multilingual models
papers.research_question: How are linguistic properties encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in multilingual models like M-BERT and XLM-R?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual models jointly encode typological linguistic properties across languages, and this can be probed using the cross-neutralising method.
papers.conclusion: Typological feature values are encoded jointly across languages in multilingual models and can be localized via language centroids.
papers.key_findings:
Self-neutralising by subtracting language centroids removes typological information, reducing probing accuracy to chance levels.
Cross-neutralising shows that performance deteriorates for languages sharing the same typological feature value, indicating joint encoding.
This joint encoding pattern is observed in both M-BERT and XLM-R models.
The effect is consistent across different layers of the models.
Language centroids capture specific feature values in a localizable way across languages.
papers.limitation: When probing performance before neutralising is low (<75% accuracy), it is unclear what information the language centroids capture, limiting the interpretation of results.
future_direction: Correlate typological feature encoding with downstream task performance
Use cross-neutralising for selective generalization in models based on typology
Apply the method to other scenarios like multimodal models
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders are widely used to transfer NLP models across languages. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model's ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, little is known as to how these models are able to do this. We propose a simple method to study how relationships between languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models (i.e. M-BERT and XLM-R). The results provide insight into their information sharing mechanisms and suggest that linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in these models.

papers.title: First Align, then Predict: Understanding the Cross-Lingual Ability of Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: What parts of the model and what mechanisms support zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual BERT?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT operates as the stacking of two modules: a multilingual encoder in the lower layers critical for cross-lingual transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little importance for transfer.
papers.conclusion: mBERT is constructed from a multilingual encoder in the lower layers that aligns representations across languages and is critical for cross-language transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little effect on transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of mBERT are critical for cross-lingual transfer, while upper layers are task-specific and language-agnostic.
Cross-lingual similarity (CKA) between representations of source and target languages is highest in the middle layers and strongly correlates with cross-lingual performance.
Randomly initializing lower layers harms cross-lingual performance but not same-language performance, indicating their specific role in cross-lingual alignment.
The cross-lingual alignment learned during pretraining is preserved after fine-tuning.
This mechanism suggests mBERT reproduces the standard cross-lingual pipeline without explicit supervision.
future_direction: Using the findings to design better multilingual pre-training processes.
Inspecting the mismatch with Singh et al. (2019) who found no language alignment across layers for Natural Language Inference.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot crosslingual transfer capabilities. Such transfer emerges by fine-tuning on a task of interest in one language and evaluating on a distinct language, not seen during the fine-tuning. Despite promising results, we still lack a proper understanding of the source of this transfer. Using a novel layer ablation technique and analyses of the model's internal representations, we show that multilingual BERT, a popular multilingual language model, can be viewed as the stacking of two sub-networks: a multilingual encoder followed by a taskspecific language-agnostic predictor. While the encoder is crucial for cross-lingual transfer and remains mostly unchanged during finetuning, the task predictor has little importance on the transfer and can be reinitialized during fine-tuning. We present extensive experiments with three distinct tasks, seventeen typologically diverse languages and multiple domains to support our hypothesis.

papers.title: Finding Universal Grammatical Relations in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: To what extent does Multilingual BERT learn a cross-lingual representation of syntactic structure? Does mBERT learn universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations; its syntactic subspaces are shared across languages and capture dependency clusters that largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, indicating the model induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations and induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision, which largely agree with the dependency labels of Universal Dependencies.
papers.key_findings:
The structural probe recovers syntactic tree distances in multiple languages from mBERT representations.
The syntactic subspaces are shared across languages, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of syntactic information.
mBERT represents dependency clusters that largely overlap with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, showing it learns universal grammatical relations.
The cross-lingual syntactic subspace is a small part (approx. 32-128 dimensions) of the overall 768-dimensional representation.
Transfer probe performance is substantially correlated with subspace similarity across languages.
papers.limitation:
Cannot tease apart whether transfer performance is caused by subword overlap or by a more fundamental sharing of parameters.
Only conduct a qualitative study in the unsupervised emergence of dependency labels via t-SNE; future work could extend to quantitative results.
Acknowledge issues in interpreting t-SNE plots.
Methods cannot support causal implications for the decisions made by the model.
future_direction: Explore other multilingual models like XLM and XLM-RoBERTa.
Attempt to understand the extent to which the discovered properties have causal implications for the model's decisions.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found evidence that Multilingual BERT (mBERT), a transformer-based multilingual masked language model, is capable of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, suggesting that some aspects of its representations are shared cross-lingually. To better understand this overlap, we extend recent work on finding syntactic trees in neural networks' internal representations to the multilingual setting. We show that subspaces of mBERT representations recover syntactic tree distances in languages other than English, and that these subspaces are approximately shared across languages. Motivated by these results, we present an unsupervised analysis method that provides evidence mBERT learns representations of syntactic dependency labels, in the form of clusters which largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy. This evidence suggests that even without explicit supervision, multilingual masked language models learn certain linguistic universals.

papers.title: Focusing on Language: Revealing and Exploiting Language Attention Heads in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs? Specifically, are there language-specific and language-general attention heads, and how can they be used to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LAHIS, a method to identify language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs, and shows how modulating these heads can control cross-lingual attention and improve multilingual performance with minimal parameters.
papers.conclusion: The work enhances interpretability of multilingual behaviors in LLMs from the perspective of MHA and presents practical approaches to strengthen multilingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LAHIS reveals the existence of language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs.
Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer, allowing steering of model attention to target languages.
Modulating language-specific heads mitigates off-target language generation by suppressing English-heads.
A lightweight adaptation using a trainable matrix on language-specific heads improves multilingual question answering accuracy with only 14-20 parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support multilingual understanding and generation. Meanwhile, efforts to interpret their internal mechanisms have emerged, offering insights to enhance multilingual performance. While multi-head self-attention (MHA) has proven critical in many areas, its role in multilingual capabilities remains underexplored. In this work, we study the contribution of MHA in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs. We propose Language Attention Head Importance Scores (LAHIS), an effective and efficient method that identifies attention head importance for multilingual capabilities via a single forward and backward pass through the LLM. Applying LAHIS to Aya-23-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, we reveal the existence of both language-specific and language-general heads. Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer to guide the model toward target language contexts and mitigate off-target language generation issue, contributing to addressing challenges in multilingual LLMs. We also introduce a lightweight adaptation that learns a soft head mask to modulate attention outputs over language heads, requiring only 20 tunable parameters to improve XQuAD accuracy. Overall, our work enhances both the interpretability and multilingual capabilities of LLMs from the perspective of MHA.

papers.title: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.research_question: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.core_contribution: Injecting linguistic structure bias into language models via guided attention during fine-tuning can improve alignment with brain recordings, particularly for word-level fMRI data.
papers.conclusion: Injecting linguistic structure bias through guided attention can improve brain decoding performance, with clearer benefits for finer-grained (word-level) analyses, and highlights the importance of controlling for domain effects.
papers.key_findings:
For the word-level Wehbe2014 fMRI dataset, guided attention models significantly outperform pretrained and domain-finetuned baselines in brain decoding.
For the sentence-level Pereira2018 dataset, improvements are more modest, with UD and DM guided attention models showing some improvement over the pretrained baseline.
Domain of the fine-tuning data is an important confound affecting brain alignment; simply fine-tuning on a different domain can reduce alignment.
Guided attention models perform better on subject-verb agreement syntactic probing tasks, with performance ranking corresponding to brain decoding scores.
Guided attention improves performance on a semantic tagging task for most semantic categories, especially discourse and temporal relations.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI data was recorded during passive reading without a specific task, which may limit the ability to uncover fine-grained patterns of linguistic structure.
Potential confounds such as domain, corpus size, and dependency length differences between the linguistic formalisms are not fully controlled for due to the lack of a common annotated corpus.
future_direction: Investigating brain alignment using continuous, naturalistic listening fMRI datasets.
Using a common annotated corpus for all formalisms to properly control for confounds like domain and corpus size.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists evaluate deep neural networks for natural language processing as possible candidate models for how language is processed in the brain. These models are often trained without explicit linguistic supervision, but have been shown to learn some linguistic structure in the absence of such supervision (Manning et al., 2020), potentially questioning the relevance of symbolic linguistic theories in modeling such cognitive processes (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). We evaluate across two fMRI datasets whether language models align better with brain recordings, if their attention is biased by annotations from syntactic or semantic formalisms. Using structure from dependency or minimal recursion semantic annotations, we find alignments improve significantly for one of the datasets. For another dataset, we see more mixed results. We present an extensive analysis of these results. Our proposed approach enables the evaluation of more targeted hypotheses about the composition of meaning in the brain, expanding the range of possible scientific inferences a neuroscientist could make, and opens up new opportunities for cross-pollination between computational neuroscience and linguistics.

papers.title: Do Attention Heads in BERT Track Syntactic Dependencies?
papers.research_question: Do attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa implicitly capture syntactic dependency relations?
papers.core_contribution: Some attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa specialize in tracking specific syntactic dependency types, but no single head performs holistic parsing well, and fine-tuning has limited impact on attention patterns.
papers.conclusion: Certain specialist attention heads track specific dependency types, but no generalist heads exist for holistic parsing, and fine-tuning does not significantly change attention patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Some attention heads capture dependency types like nsubj and obj with high accuracy compared to baselines.
No attention head forms complete parse trees effectively, as shown by the MST method.
Fine-tuning on MNLI improves accuracy for long-distance clausal dependencies but degrades short-distance ones.
Fine-tuning on CoLA does not significantly affect dependency tracking accuracy.
Attention weights do not fully reflect the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.
papers.limitation:
Analyzing attention weights directly may not reveal much of the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.
Using the gold root in the MST method may artificially improve results, though bias is applied evenly.
papers.abstract: We investigate the extent to which individual attention heads in pretrained transformer language models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, implicitly capture syntactic dependency relations. We employ two methods---taking the maximum attention weight and computing the maximum spanning tree---to extract implicit dependency relations from the attention weights of each layer/head, and compare them to the ground-truth Universal Dependency (UD) trees. We show that, for some UD relation types, there exist heads that can recover the dependency type significantly better than baselines on parsed English text, suggesting that some self-attention heads act as a proxy for syntactic structure. We also analyze BERT fine-tuned on two datasets---the syntax-oriented CoLA and the semantics-oriented MNLI---to investigate whether fine-tuning affects the patterns of their self-attention, but we do not observe substantial differences in the overall dependency relations extracted using our methods. Our results suggest that these models have some specialist attention heads that track individual dependency types, but no generalist head that performs holistic parsing significantly better than a trivial baseline, and that analyzing attention weights directly may not reveal much of the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.

papers.title: Syntactic Analysis in Transformers through Attention Heads
papers.research_question: Does BERTimbau, a monolingual Brazilian Portuguese Transformer model, exhibit attention head specialization aligned with core syntactic relations such as subject-verb dependencies?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies specialized attention heads in BERTimbau for syntactic dependencies, with Layer 2 Head 3 as a general-purpose subject-verb tracker, and shows that monolingual training yields more focused syntactic encoding than multilingual models.
papers.conclusion: BERTimbau's attention heads are specialized for syntactic dependencies, with Layer 2 Head 3 as a consistent tracker, and monolingual models like BERTimbau have more focused syntactic attention than multilingual models like mBERT.
papers.key_findings:
Layer 2, Head 3 (L2 H3) consistently captures subject-verb dependencies across various grammatical constructions.
Other heads exhibit context-specific specialization, such as L6 H11 for subordinate clauses and L7 H12 for reflexive structures.
BERTimbau demonstrates lower entropy and higher syntactic scores in top heads compared to mBERT, indicating more stable syntactic attention.
Attention patterns align with syntactic functions rather than lexical categories, supporting the role of attention in encoding grammatical relations.
The model shows robustness to syntactic reordering, maintaining attention in non-canonical word orders.
papers.limitation:
The analysis did not address more complex word-order alternations such as raising constructions.
The dataset is limited to 42 sentences, which may constrain generalizability.
Attention weights are correlational and do not guarantee causal interpretation of syntactic encoding.
future_direction: Analyze complex word-order alternations such as raising constructions.
Expand the dataset beyond 42 sentences for more robust statistical validation.
Probe causal mechanisms via ablation studies and causal probing experiments.
papers.abstract: The advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have led to the development of Transformer architectures, such as BERT. One of the most prominent features of this architecture is the attention mechanism. However, the application of attention mechanisms to languages other than English, like Brazilian Portuguese, remains underexplored. This work analyzes the attention heads in a Transformer architecture, considering the syntactic relations in a sentence. We analyze how attention patterns align with syntactic dependencies involving phenomena such as transitive verbs, reflexive pronouns, and subordinate clauses, as realized in Brazilian Portuguese. Results described the existence of specialized heads within arcs, such as subject–verb and verb–object. These findings open up new research opportunities to evaluate syntactic sensitivity in Transformer models and to contribute to the development of more linguistically informed models for Brazilian Portuguese.

papers.title: Discovering Language-neutral Sub-networks in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual pre-trained language models learn language-neutral representations, and what is the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models contain language-neutral sub-networks that are topologically similar across languages and can be effectively transferred for cross-lingual tasks, but this transferability decreases at higher sparsity levels.
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that multilingual language models include separate language-neutral and language-specific components, with the language-neutral components playing a more prominent role in cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.key_findings:
Winning tickets (sub-networks) can be found for each language and task at multiple sparsity levels, though performance degrades at higher sparsity.
Sub-networks for different languages have high parameter overlap, especially for NER and XNLI tasks, indicating language-neutral components.
Cross-lingual transfer of winning tickets is effective for XNLI and NER, but less so for MLM, and transfer performance degrades at higher sparsity.
The language-neutral components are more prominent in the middle to upper layers of the model.
Combining multiple languages during pruning can yield sub-networks that transfer better to low-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Parameter overlap may not be a fine-grained measure for identifying language-neutral components, as small differences in cross-lingual performance do not strongly correlate with overlap.
Only the lottery ticket hypothesis is used for discovering sub-networks, while other pruning and masking methods may provide complementary or competing insights.
Due to computational limitations, the analysis is limited to three tasks and eleven languages, and new insights may emerge from a larger cross-section.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pre-trained language models transfer remarkably well on cross-lingual downstream tasks. However, the extent to which they learn language-neutral representations (i.e., shared representations that encode similar phenomena across languages), and the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance, remain open questions. In this work, we conceptualize language neutrality of multilingual models as a function of the overlap between language-encoding subnetworks of these models. We employ the lottery ticket hypothesis to discover sub-networks that are individually optimized for various languages and tasks. Our evaluation across three distinct tasks and eleven typologically-diverse languages demonstrates that sub-networks for different languages are topologically similar (i.e., language-neutral), making them effective initializations for cross-lingual transfer with limited performance degradation. 1

papers.title: A multilabel approach to morphosyntactic probing
papers.research_question: How well does multilingual BERT encode morphosyntactic features across languages, and which features are recognized as shared cross-linguistically?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a multilabel probing paradigm for morphosyntactic analysis and demonstrates that multilingual BERT encodes many morphosyntactic features extractably, with some features shared cross-linguistically.
papers.conclusion: Multilabel probing is an effective method for analyzing morphosyntactic representations in multilingual language models, revealing that mBERT encodes many features and that some are represented cross-linguistically.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT-6 holds the most morphosyntactic information, with probes achieving micro-averaged F1 scores between 0.83 and 0.97 for seven languages.
Multilingual probes slightly underperform monolingual probes but exhibit better selectivity, suggesting less memorization.
Cross-lingual transfer experiments show that nouns and verbs are well transferred, while adjectives and nominative case are less consistently recognized across languages.
The multilabel paradigm enables fine-grained analysis of feature co-occurrence and agreement patterns, as demonstrated in a case study of Hebrew determiners.
Probe performance varies across languages due to differences in feature sets and training set sizes, making direct comparison difficult.
papers.limitation: The UD corpora used are from narrow domains (e.g., Wikipedia, news, Bible) and may not capture the full range of linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Probe different multilingual language models to compare their morphosyntactic representations.
Explore how global and feature-level probe performance corresponds to downstream task performance.
Conduct more detailed analyses of specific features and their cross-linguistic transfer.
papers.abstract: We propose using a multilabel probing task to assess the morphosyntactic representations of multilingual word embeddings. This tweak on canonical probing makes it easy to explore morphosyntactic representations, both holistically and at the level of individual features (e.g., gender, number, case), and leads more naturally to the study of how language models handle co-occurring features (e.g., agreement phenomena). We demonstrate this task with multilingual BERT Through this simple but robust paradigm, we verify that multilingual BERT renders many morphosyntactic features simultaneously extractable. We further evaluate the probes on six held-out languages: Arabic, Chinese, Marathi, Slovenian, Tagalog, and Yorb. This zero-shot style of probing has the added benefit of revealing which cross-linguistic properties a language model recognizes as being shared by multiple languages.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: Can you map it to English? The Role of Cross-Lingual Alignment in Multilingual Performance of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on NLU tasks, and does misalignment causally explain failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cross-lingual alignment with English in middle layers is associated with and causally affects LLM performance on multilingual NLU tasks.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual semantic alignment in localized middle layers contributes causally to non-English correctness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer Success (TS) instances exhibit higher cross-lingual alignment with English than Transfer Failure (TF) instances.
Activation patching of English activations into non-English forward passes can correct incorrect predictions, indicating causal role of alignment.
Middle layers (e.g., layers 16-25) are critical for alignment and effective patching.
Control patching experiments show that semantic alignment, not just target token bias, drives corrections in specific middle layers.
Alignment peaks in middle layers and varies by language typology, with closer languages to English showing higher alignment.
papers.limitation:
Scope restricted to discriminative NLU tasks.
Benchmarks may have translation artifacts due to human translation from English.
Only analyzes bilingual alignment with English, not between other languages.
future_direction: Exploring targeted steering at inference time to leverage English activations for enhancing performance on non-English languages.
Studying potential downsides such as inflated confidence and erasure of valuable local, non-English knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer prompts in many languages, despite being trained predominantly on English; yet, the mechanisms driving this generalization remain poorly understood. This work asks: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on natural language understanding (NLU) tasks? We study the role of representation alignment in instance-level task decisions, complementing prior analyses conducted both at the language level and task-independently. We introduce the Discriminative Alignment Index ($\DALI$) to quantify instance-level alignment across 24 languages other than English and three distinct NLU tasks. Results show that incorrect NLU predictions are strongly associated with lower representation alignment with English in the model's middle layers.
