Through activation patching, we show that incorrect predictions in languages other than English can be fixed by patching their parallel English activations in the middle layers, thereby demonstrating the causal role of representation (mis)alignment in cross-lingual correctness.

papers.title: Probing the Emergence of Cross-lingual Alignment during LLM Training
papers.research_question: How does cross-lingual alignment emerge during the pre-training of multilingual large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a strong correlation between cross-lingual neuron overlap and zero-shot transfer performance in multilingual LLMs, and reveals non-monotonic alignment dynamics during pre-training with drops in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that shared neurons encoding linguistic features are tightly connected to cross-lingual transfer ability, providing insights into multilingual pretraining dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron overlap for linguistic features increases during pre-training but experiences severe drops in smaller model scales like BLOOM560m and BLOOM1b1.
There is a statistically significant, strong correlation between neuron overlap and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on tasks like POS tagging and XNLI.
Larger models (e.g., BLOOM1b7) show more monotonic growth in alignment, suggesting a scaling law effect.
Drops in alignment correspond to degradation in both in-language and cross-lingual performance.
The emergence of cross-lingual alignment is not steady and can pass through sub-optimal regions during training.
papers.limitation:
Focus on BLOOM checkpoints with large intervals, so findings might not apply to finer-grained training windows.
Only consider autoregressive models with the same objective and training dataset; varying these may result in different patterns.
Focus on alignment of languages seen during pretraining, leaving generalization to unseen languages for future research.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable levels of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance. We speculate that this is predicated on their ability to align languages without explicit supervision from parallel sentences. While representations of translationally equivalent sentences in different languages are known to be similar after convergence, however, it remains unclear how such cross-lingual alignment emerges during pre-training of LLMs. Our study leverages intrinsic probing techniques, which identify which subsets of neurons encode linguistic features, to correlate the degree of cross-lingual neuron overlap with the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance for a given model. In particular, we rely on checkpoints of BLOOM, a multilingual autoregressive LLM, across different training steps and model scales. We observe a high correlation between neuron overlap and downstream performance, which supports our hypothesis on the conditions leading to effective cross-lingual transfer. Interestingly, we also detect a degradation of both implicit alignment and multilingual abilities in certain phases of the pre-training process, providing new insights into the multilingual pretraining dynamics.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: Probing LLMs for Joint Encoding of Linguistic Categories
papers.research_question: How are linguistically related syntactic categories jointly encoded in LLMs, and do these patterns hold across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence that linguistically related syntactic categories are jointly encoded in LLMs, with similar patterns across languages and between different levels of the linguistic hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates joint encoding of linguistic categories in LLMs, supporting the idea that models learn hierarchical and shared representations for syntax across languages.
papers.key_findings:
POS tags that are linguistically related are jointly encoded in both monolingual and multilingual models.
Joint encoding patterns are consistent across English, Italian, and Greek in multilingual models.
Information about linguistic categories can be shared across languages, indicating language-agnostic encoding.
There is evidence of joint encoding between POS tags and dependency relations, suggesting information sharing across tasks.
The cross-neutralization method effectively reveals shared representations without tuning the base models.
papers.limitation:
Limited to encoder-only architectures.
Only three languages are examined.
Limited to syntactic tasks (POS tagging and dependency labeling).
Lack of cross-neutralization effects does not necessarily indicate absence of joint encoding.
future_direction: Extend experiments to more languages, particularly low-resource and typologically distant languages.
Include higher-level semantic tasks such as semantic role labeling and coreference resolution.
Explore other model architectures like encoder-decoder or decoder-only models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive performance on a range of NLP tasks, due to the general-purpose linguistic knowledge acquired during pretraining. Existing model interpretability research (Tenney et al., 2019) suggests that a linguistic hierarchy emerges in the LLM layers, with lower layers better suited to solving syntactic tasks and higher layers employed for semantic processing. Yet, little is known about how encodings of different linguistic phenomena interact within the models and to what extent processing of linguistically-related categories relies on the same, shared model representations. In this paper, we propose a framework for testing the joint encoding of linguistic categories in LLMs. Focusing on syntax, we find evidence of joint encoding both at the same (related part-of-speech (POS) classes) and different (POS classes and related syntactic dependency relations) levels of linguistic hierarchy. Our cross-lingual experiments show that the same patterns hold across languages in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how factual knowledge is acquired and represented in multilingual language models, examining performance differences across languages, shared vs. independent representations, and mechanisms of cross-lingual transfer.
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies three patterns of fact representation in multilingual language models—language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred—and reveals limited effectiveness of cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge and underscores the need for better representation learning and probing datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance varies across languages with moderate correlation to training data volume.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations based on neuron activity patterns.
Cross-lingual knowledge transfer is limited and often localized to geographically proximate languages.
Easy-to-predict facts include shared entity tokens and naming cues, reducing apparent cross-lingual transfer.
Active neurons for facts in low-resource languages are more distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R), and findings may not generalize to decoder-based models like BLOOM.
future_direction: Enhance cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs). In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge. Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT). We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts. We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: language-independent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them. Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While previous studies point out this cross-lingual inconsistency issue, the underlying causes remain unexplored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability methods to investigate cross-lingual inconsistencies in MLMs. We find that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, and only transition to language-specific spaces in the final layers. Failures during the language transition often result in incorrect predictions in the target language, even when the answers are correct in other languages. To mitigate this inconsistency issue, we propose a linear shortcut method that bypasses computations in the final layers, enhancing both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency. Our findings shed light on the internal mechanisms of MLMs and provide a lightweight, effective strategy for producing more consistent factual outputs.

papers.title: Semantic Pivots Enable Cross-Lingual Transfer in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to quantify, understand, and improve the cross-lingual ability of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a word-level cross-lingual translation task and dataset (CLWTD) to quantify cross-lingual ability, identifies co-occurrence and semantic pivot behaviors in LLMs, links them to dataset co-occurrence, and shows that constructing a semantic pivot-aware pre-training dataset improves cross-lingual ability.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a word-level task to quantify cross-lingual ability, identifies and distinguishes two behaviors, attributes them to co-occurrence frequency, finds semantic pivots from the dataset, and improves cross-lingual ability by reconstructing a pre-training dataset.
papers.key_findings:
The Cross-Lingual Word Translation Dataset (CLWTD) provides a continuous metric that accurately reflects LLMs' cross-lingual ability.
LLMs exhibit two distinct behaviors during word translation: co-occurrence behavior and semantic pivot behavior.
These behaviors are attributed to the co-occurrence frequency of words in the pre-training dataset.
Semantic pivots can be identified from the pre-training data and show a probability trend in intermediate layers.
Constructing a pre-training dataset with a high proportion of semantic pivots effectively enhances cross-lingual ability.
papers.limitation: Due to limited availability of open-source large language models with public checkpoints and pre-training data, experiments are only validated on the OLMo-1B model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable ability in cross-lingual tasks. Understanding how LLMs acquire this ability is crucial for their interpretability. To quantify the cross-lingual ability of LLMs accurately, we propose a Word-Level Cross-Lingual Translation Task. To find how LLMs learn cross-lingual ability, we trace the outputs of LLMs' intermediate layers in the word translation task. We identify and distinguish two distinct behaviors in the forward pass of LLMs: co-occurrence behavior and semantic pivot behavior. We attribute LLMs' two distinct behaviors to the co-occurrence frequency of words and find the semantic pivot from the pre-training dataset. Finally, to apply our findings to improve the cross-lingual ability of LLMs, we reconstruct a semantic pivot-aware pre-training dataset using documents with a high proportion of semantic pivots. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing cross-lingual ability. Our research contributes insights into the interpretability of LLMs and offers a method for improving LLMs' cross-lingual ability.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Does multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, with neuron overlap varying by category and influenced by language proximity and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models implicitly align morphosyntactic information across languages by using overlapping subsets of neurons, which may affect their cross-lingual transfer capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Significant cross-lingual overlap exists in neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
Overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and is lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Overlap is higher for languages within the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with pre-training data size but decreases with larger model size (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
XLM-R-base tends to share more neurons than m-BERT for encoding morphosyntactic attributes.
future_direction: Artificially encouraging neuron overlap to facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models. 1

papers.title: Multilingual Probing of Deep Pre-Trained Contextual Encoders
papers.research_question: What linguistic information do multilingual pre-trained contextual encoders retain, and how does this information vary across languages, encoders, and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive multilingual evaluation of pre-trained encoders using probing tasks, revealing that recurrent architectures (ELMo) better retain lower-level linguistic information than self-attentive ones (BERT, XLM), and that cross-lingual training (XLM) leads to a loss of language-specific linguistic details.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful method for comparing encoders across languages, and the choice of encoder architecture and training objective significantly affects what linguistic information is retained, with cross-lingual models sacrificing language-specific details.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrent architectures (ELMo) retain lower-level linguistic phenomena (e.g., sentence length, word count) better than self-attentive architectures (BERT, XLM).
XLM performs worse on most probing tasks compared to BERT and ELMo, likely due to its cross-lingual training objective causing a loss of language-specific information.
For semantic tasks, the performance gap between recurrent and self-attentive architectures is smaller.
Language-specific differences exist; for example, French and Spanish perform better on subject and object number tasks due to morphological marking.
The results do not indicate that English is better represented in the multilingual models than the other languages studied.
papers.limitation:
Use of non-gold-standard dependency parses for some languages may introduce inaccuracies in the probing data.
The probing tasks are limited and do not include many truly semantic tasks.
future_direction: Designing more semantic-level probing tasks, possibly using cross-lingual semantic resources like the Parallel Meaning Bank.
Extending the evaluation to more languages and tasks.
papers.abstract: Encoders that generate representations based on context have, in recent years, benefited from adaptations that allow for pre-training on large text corpora. Earlier work on evaluating fixed-length sentence representations has included the use of ‘probing’ tasks, that use diagnostic classifiers to attempt to quantify the extent to which these encoders capture specific linguistic phenomena. The principle of probing has also resulted in extended evaluations that include relatively newer word-level pre-trained encoders. We build on probing tasks established in the literature and comprehensively evaluate and analyse – from a typological perspective amongst others – multilingual variants of existing encoders on probing datasets constructed for 6 non-English languages. Specifically, we probe each layer of a multiple monolingual RNN-based ELMo models, the transformer-based BERT’s cased and uncased multilingual variants, and a variant of BERT that uses a cross-lingual modelling scheme (XLM).

papers.title: Analyzing the Structure of Attention in a Transformer Language Model
papers.research_question: Does attention align with syntactic dependency relations? Which attention heads attend to which part-of-speech tags? How does attention capture long-distance relationships versus short-distance ones?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes attention in the GPT-2 Transformer language model, finding that attention heads specialize in particular part-of-speech tags at different layers, attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in middle layers, and the deepest layers capture the most distant relationships.
papers.conclusion: The structure of attention in GPT-2 is closely tied to the language modeling objective, with attention patterns often focusing on words relevant for predicting the next token. The analysis provides human-interpretable descriptions of model behavior and is complementary to linguistic probing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model.
Attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers.
The deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships.
Attention heads exhibit specific patterns, such as focusing on acronyms, place names, or head nouns, as revealed by exemplar sentences.
Attention variability distinguishes content-dependent from content-independent (position-based) heads.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Wikipedia text, which has a specific encyclopedic format and style, so it is unclear how attention patterns manifest in other types of content.
Attention may not fully explain individual model predictions, as noted by recent work (Jain and Wallace, 2019).
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other Transformer models such as BERT, which has a bidirectional architecture and is trained on both token-level and sentence-level tasks.
Analyze attention patterns in other types of content, such as dialog scripts or song lyrics.
Analyze attention patterns in longer texts, especially for new Transformer variants like Transformer-XL and Sparse Transformer.
papers.abstract: The Transformer is a fully attention-based alternative to recurrent networks that has achieved state-of-the-art results across a range of NLP tasks. In this paper, we analyze the structure of attention in a Transformer language model, the GPT-2 small pretrained model. We visualize attention for individual instances and analyze the interaction between attention and syntax over a large corpus. We find that attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model, and that attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers. We also find that the deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships. Finally, we extract exemplar sentences that reveal highly specific patterns targeted by particular attention heads.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Studying the Inductive Biases of RNNs with Synthetic Variations of Natural Languages
papers.research_question: How do typological properties such as word order and morphological case marking affect the ability of neural sequence models to acquire the syntax of a language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for generating synthetic languages by parametrically modifying parsed corpora to study the inductive biases of RNNs, and uses it to show that RNNs have a recency bias, that polypersonal agreement improves performance, and that overt case marking facilitates agreement prediction.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methodology is effective for studying grammatical inductive biases of RNNs, and the findings reveal that RNNs exhibit a recency bias, benefit from multitask agreement prediction, and are aided by case marking.
papers.key_findings:
Performance was higher in subject-verb-object order (SVO) than in subject-object-verb order (SOV), suggesting that RNNs have a recency bias.
Predicting agreement with both subject and object (polypersonal agreement) improves over predicting each separately, suggesting that underlying syntactic knowledge transfers across tasks.
Overt morphological case makes agreement prediction significantly easier, regardless of word order.
papers.limitation:
The reordering manipulation is limited to core elements (subjects, objects, and verbs) and does not consider word order inside other types of phrases.
The synthetic languages are simpler than natural languages because word order is completely fixed or fully flexible, while natural languages often have more complex and varied word order patterns.
future_direction: Exploring whether consistent reordering across phrase categories (head directionality parameter) improves model performance.
Conducting human experiments based on the agreement prediction task to compare human and RNN learning.
papers.abstract: How do typological properties such as word order and morphological case marking affect the ability of neural sequence models to acquire the syntax of a language? Cross-linguistic comparisons of RNNs' syntactic performance (e.g., on subject-verb agreement prediction) are complicated by the fact that any two languages differ in multiple typological properties, as well as by differences in training corpus. We propose a paradigm that addresses these issues: we create synthetic versions of English, which differ from English in one or more typological parameters, and generate corpora for those languages based on a parsed English corpus. We report a series of experiments in which RNNs were trained to predict agreement features for verbs in each of those synthetic languages. Among other findings, (1) performance was higher in subject-verb-object order (as in English) than in subject-object-verb order (as in Japanese), suggesting that RNNs have a recency bias; (2) predicting agreement with both subject and object (polypersonal agreement) improves over predicting each separately, suggesting that underlying syntactic knowledge transfers across the two tasks; and (3) overt morphological case makes agreement prediction significantly easier, regardless of word order.

papers.title: How Does Selective Mechanism Improve Self-Attention Networks?
papers.research_question: How does the selective mechanism improve self-attention networks (SANs)? Specifically, what are the underlying reasons for the strong performance of selective SANs?
papers.core_contribution: The selective mechanism, implemented via Gumbel-Softmax, improves self-attention networks by mitigating their weaknesses in word order encoding and syntactic structure modeling, primarily by focusing attention on semantically important content words.
papers.conclusion: The selective mechanism mitigates two major weaknesses of self-attention networks—word order encoding and structure modeling—by enabling the model to focus on content words, which is essential for natural language understanding and generation.
papers.key_findings:
SSANs consistently outperform standard SANs on multiple NLP tasks (natural language inference, semantic role labeling, machine translation).
SSANs improve the ability to capture both local and global word order information, as shown by higher accuracy on word reordering detection tasks.
SSANs produce more syntactic representations and better model sentence structure, as evidenced by improved performance on linguistic probing tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst).
The selective mechanism helps SANs by paying more attention to content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and less to function words (prepositions, determiners, punctuation).
Applying the selective mechanism to the first encoder layer yields the most significant improvements for word order tasks, suggesting lexical information is crucial.
papers.limitation: The findings are validated on specific SAN architectures and tasks; their generalizability to other architectures (e.g., BERT) and more general attention models remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validating the findings on other SAN architectures (e.g., BERT).
Extending the analysis to more general attention models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention networks (SANs) with selective mechanism has produced substantial improvements in various NLP tasks by concentrating on a subset of input words. However, the underlying reasons for their strong performance have not been well explained. In this paper, we bridge the gap by assessing the strengths of selective SANs (SSANs), which are implemented with a flexible and universal Gumbel-Softmax. Experimental results on several representative NLP tasks, including natural language inference, semantic role labelling, and machine translation, show that SSANs consistently outperform the standard SANs. Through well-designed probing experiments, we empirically validate that the improvement of SSANs can be attributed in part to mitigating two commonly-cited weaknesses of SANs: word order encoding and structure modeling. Specifically, the selective mechanism improves SANs by paying more attention to content words that contribute to the meaning of the sentence. The code and data are released at https://github.com/xwgeng/SSAN.

papers.title: Converging to a Lingua Franca: Evolution of Linguistic Regions and Semantics Alignment in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally achieve cross-lingual skill transfer through neuron activation patterns and semantic alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual LLMs develop a common semantic latent space ('Lingua Franca') for processing inputs across languages, with alignment improving through training and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide insights into the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling, offering a foundation for improving cross-lingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron activation patterns are similar for inputs in the same language, revealing key linguistic regions that can be identified and deactivated to impair language-specific performance.
Activation patterns are similar for semantically identical sentences in different languages, indicating mapping to a common semantic space ('Lingua Franca').
With training, key linguistic regions become smaller and activation patterns become more language-agnostic.
Semantic alignment strengthens with training and increased model size, enhancing cross-lingual reasoning ability.
Key neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on BLOOM and LLaMA2 models, may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on specific datasets like Bible and XL-Sum, which may not cover all linguistic nuances.
Methodology based on averaged activation patterns and z-scores may not capture all neuron interactions.
Underlying reasons for patterns remain speculative, requiring further research for causal relationships.
future_direction: Examine a broader range of multilingual LLM architectures.
Utilize more diverse datasets, including low-resource languages.
Apply more sophisticated techniques like causal inference methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, particularly in multilingual contexts. While recent studies suggest that LLMs can transfer skills learned in one language to others, the internal mechanisms behind this ability remain unclear. We observed that the neuron activation patterns of LLMs exhibit similarities when processing the same language, revealing the existence and location of key linguistic regions. Additionally, we found that neuron activation patterns are similar when processing sentences with the same semantic meaning in different languages. This indicates that LLMs map semantically identical inputs from different languages into a "Lingua Franca", a common semantic latent space that allows for consistent processing across languages. This semantic alignment becomes more pronounced with training and increased model size, resulting in a more language-agnostic activation pattern. Moreover, we found that key linguistic neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers of LLMs, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses. Experiments on BLOOM and LLaMA2 support these findings, highlighting the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling up. This paper provides insights into the internal workings of LLMs, offering a foundation for future improvements in their cross-lingual capabilities.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Models of Visually Grounded Speech Signal Pay Attention to Nouns: A Bilingual Experiment on English and Japanese
papers.research_question: What is the behavior of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on English and Japanese, and does it focus on nouns?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that attention in neural models of visually grounded speech focuses on nouns across English and Japanese, and demonstrates cross-lingual speech retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that attention in visually grounded speech models focuses on nouns across languages, with language-specific adaptations, and enables cross-lingual retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.key_findings:
Attention primarily focuses on nouns in both English and Japanese models.
The Japanese model also pays attention to particles, developing a language-specific behavior similar to human toddlers.
Attention peaks are located at word endings in English and at both beginnings and endings in Japanese.
Images can be used as pivots for cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval without parallel data.
The model exhibits noun-bias, aligning with theories of child language acquisition.
papers.limitation: The study uses synthetic speech with only one voice, whereas prior work used real speech with multiple speakers.
future_direction: Validate the methodology on a bilingual dataset featuring real voices.
Extract a bilingual speech-to-speech dictionary using attention peaks as anchor points.
papers.abstract: We investigate the behaviour of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on two languages: English and Japanese. Experimental results show that attention focuses on nouns and this behaviour holds true for two very typologically different languages. We also draw parallels between artificial neural attention and human attention and show that neural attention focuses on word endings as it has been theorised for human attention. Finally, we investigate how two visually grounded monolingual models can be used to perform cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval. For both languages, the enriched bilingual (speech-image) corpora with part-of-speech tags and forced alignments are distributed to the community for reproducible research.

papers.title: LINSPECTOR: Multilingual Probing Tasks for Word Representations
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate word representation models in a multilingual setting to understand what linguistic features they capture and how this correlates with downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LINSPECTOR, a set of multilingual probing tasks and an evaluation suite for word representations, and shows that probing task performance correlates with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the introduced probing tasks and the LINSPECTOR framework are effective for evaluating word representations in multiple languages and that they correlate with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.key_findings:
Probing tasks can be used to evaluate word embeddings in multiple languages and show significant positive correlation with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
All embedding models achieved their lowest score for CharacterBin, a task that requires predicting the number of characters.
D-ELMo achieves the highest scores in probing for all language-test pairs, generally followed by fastText and GloVe-BPE.
Token-level tasks may be influenced by domain and majority class biases, while type-level tasks may suffer from lack of lexical diversity and high ambiguity ratios.
The probing tasks can be used to explore word embeddings or black-box neural models for linguistic cues in a multilingual setting.
papers.limitation: Token-level tasks may be influenced by domain and majority class biases, while type-level tasks may suffer from lack of lexical diversity and high ambiguity ratios.
future_direction: Extend probing tasks to more languages and include more linguistic phenomena.
Investigate the use of probing tasks for model selection and hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Despite an ever-growing number of word representation models introduced for a large number of languages, there is a lack of a standardized technique to provide insights into what is captured by these models. Such insights would help the community to get an estimate of the downstream task performance, as well as to design more informed neural architectures, while avoiding extensive experimentation that requires substantial computational resources not all researchers have access to. A recent development in NLP is to use simple classification tasks, also called probing tasks, that test for a single linguistic feature such as part-of-speech. Existing studies mostly focus on exploring the linguistic information encoded by the continuous representations of English text. However, from a typological perspective the morphologically poor English is rather an outlier: The information encoded by the word order and function words in English is often stored on a subword, morphological level in other languages. To address this, we introduce 15 type-level probing tasks such as case marking, possession, word length, morphological tag count, and pseudoword identification for 24 languages. We present a reusable methodology for creation and evaluation of such tests in a multilingual setting, which is challenging because of a lack of resources, lower quality of tools, and differences among languages. We then present experiments on several diverse multilingual word embedding models, in which we relate the probing task performance for a diverse set of languages to a range of five classic NLP tasks: POS-tagging, dependency parsing, semantic role labeling, named entity recognition, and natural language inference. We find that a number of probing tests have significantly high positive correlation to the downstream tasks, especially for morphologically rich languages. We show that our tests can be used to explore word embeddings or black-box neural models for linguistic cues in a multilingual setting. We release the probing data sets and the evaluation suite LINSPECTOR with https://github.com/UKPLab/linspector .

papers.title: Emergent effects of scaling on the functional hierarchies within large language models
papers.research_question: What is the functional hierarchy of abstraction across layers in LLMs, and how does it change with model scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit functional hierarchies with abstraction increasing across layers, but scaling introduces deviations such as double representation peaks and anti-persistent fluctuations in attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms functional hierarchies in LLMs but reveals emergent deviations with scaling, such as double representation peaks and layer coordination, complicating interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Item-level semantics are most strongly represented in early layers (2-7), two-item relations in middle layers (8-12), and four-item analogies in later layers (10-15), consistent with an abstraction hierarchy.
Deep layers can represent narrow two-item relations from early in the context, suggesting information compression without meaningful abstraction.
In the large Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct model, representation of two-item relations and analogies shows two distinct peaks (layers 12-16 and 25-33), indicating fluctuations in abstraction level.
Adjacent layers in the large model exhibit anti-persistent fluctuations in attention outputs, with negative autocorrelation, suggesting coordinated specialization.
Buried concepts (target text followed by filler) are represented in deeper layers, showing that late layers capture global document-wide information.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of the double-peak pattern and valley in large models is unclear and requires further work.
Analyses on grammar and syntax were inconclusive and not reported, limiting insights into syntactic processing.
future_direction: Study larger models to understand scaling effects further.
Investigate the mechanisms behind the double-peak representation and layer coordination.
Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: How does BERT’s attention change when you fine-tune? An analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention change when fine-tuned? The paper investigates this through a proposed analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for testing hypotheses about how transformer models encode linguistic phenomena, using unsupervised probes, downstream control tasks, and cross-dataset consistency. Applying it to negation scope reveals evidence of the hypothesized encoding in base models but not in large models.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a procedure and analysis methods to test hypotheses about how transformer-based models encode linguistic phenomena. Applying this to negation scope finds evidence of an interpretable encoding (in-scope words attend to the negation cue) in BERT-base and RoBERTa-base, but weaker evidence in the large models.
papers.key_findings:
Before fine-tuning, several attention heads are sensitive to negation scope, with the best BERT-base head achieving an F1 of 53.8 in a fully unsupervised setting.
There is consistency in which heads are negation-sensitive across different datasets.
After fine-tuning on a negation scope task, the average sensitivity of attention heads improved over the pretrained model for all four models, but only the two base models improved more than a control task.
Attention heads that had the top F1s in the pretrained model do not have the top-ranked improvements after fine-tuning on negation scope.
The behavior of individual attention heads becomes more consistent across datasets after fine-tuning on the negation task, compared to the pretrained model and the control task, except for RoBERTa-large.
papers.limitation:
The work focuses on one interpretable way of encoding negation scope knowledge, but there could be many other ways.
The study uses a single nonlinguistic control task, but one could imagine exploring a gradient of fine-tuning tasks.
The analysis focuses primarily on the attention mechanism, but does not explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to.
future_direction: Explore other hypothesized encodings of negation scope, such as a tree of attention leading to the negation cue.
Explore attention head changes with a gradient of fine-tuning tasks that are more or less relevant to the linguistic phenomenon.
Explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to, since these form the outputs and are more directly tied to classification decisions.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models like BERT, after fine-tuning to a downstream task, have achieved high performance on a variety of NLP problems. Yet explaining their decisions is difficult despite recent work probing their internal representations. We propose a procedure and analysis methods that take a hypothesis of how a transformer-based model might encode a linguistic phenomenon, and test the validity of that hypothesis based on a comparison between knowledge-related downstream tasks with downstream control tasks, and measurement of cross-dataset consistency. We apply this methodology to test BERT and RoBERTa on a hypothesis that some attention heads will consistently attend from a word in negation scope to the negation cue. We find that after fine-tuning BERT and RoBERTa on a negation scope task, the average attention head improves its sensitivity to negation and its attention consistency across negation datasets compared to the pre-trained models. However, only the base models (not the large models) improve compared to a control task, indicating there is evidence for a shallow encoding of negation only in the base models.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders Cross-Lingual Performance
papers.research_question: How do language models generalize knowledge to multiple languages, and why do they produce inconsistent outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs tend to reason in language-specific subspaces, hindering cross-lingual consistency and transfer, while smaller models rely on a shared English-aligned semantic space; steering smaller models towards this shared space improves their multilingual performance.
papers.conclusion: The use of shared semantic space facilitates cross-lingual transfer, and inducing processing in this space can improve multilingual reasoning in smaller models.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models are more accurate but less consistent across languages.
Cross-lingual representation similarity predicts knowledge transfer and consistency.
Larger models operate more in language-specific subspaces, while smaller models use a shared English-aligned space.
Cross-lingual activation steering towards English improves performance and consistency in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
The steering method is only tested on multi-choice questions and requires extraction of language-specific activation vectors, which may not generalize to other use cases.
The method may reinforce cultural and linguistic biases towards English.
future_direction: Develop more comprehensive methods to encode knowledge of different languages in the shared semantic space.
Address the limitation of reinforcing English bias in multilingual models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are demonstrably capable of cross-lingual transfer, but can produce inconsistent output when prompted with the same queries written in different languages. To understand how language models are able to generalize knowledge from one language to the others, we measure representation similarity between languages, and apply the logit lens to interpret the implicit steps taken by LLMs to solve multilingual multi-choice reasoning questions. Our analyses reveal LLMs predict inconsistently and are less accurate because they rely on representations that are dissimilar across languages, rather than working in a shared semantic space. While larger models are more multilingual, we show their hidden states are more likely to dissociate from the shared representation compared to smaller models, but are nevertheless more capable of retrieving knowledge embedded across different languages. Finally, we demonstrate that knowledge sharing in small models can be facilitated by steering their latent processing towards the shared semantic space. This improves the models' multilingual reasoning performance, as a result of more knowledge transfer from, and better output consistency with English.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
