Different model architectures (encoder-only vs. decoder-only) store factual knowledge in distinct locations within the network.
The language used for fine-tuning significantly affects editing performance and the location of stored knowledge.
Traditional fine-tuning (FT) can be more effective than hypernetwork-based METs in achieving higher performance in cross-lingual settings.
future_direction: Further research and development of cross-lingual model editing techniques
papers.abstract: The training of large language models (LLMs) necessitates substantial data and computational resources, and updating outdated LLMs entails significant efforts and resources. While numerous model editing techniques (METs) have emerged to efficiently update model outputs without retraining, their effectiveness in multilingual LLMs, where knowledge is stored in diverse languages, remains an underexplored research area. This research paper introduces the cross-lingual model editing (\textbf{XME}) paradigm, wherein a fact is edited in one language, and the subsequent update propagation is observed across other languages. To investigate the XME paradigm, we conducted experiments using BLOOM, mBERT, and XLM-RoBERTa using the two writing scripts: \textit{Latin} (English, French, and Spanish) and \textit{Indic} (Hindi, Gujarati, and Bengali). The results reveal notable performance limitations of state-of-the-art METs under the XME setting, mainly when the languages involved belong to two distinct script families. These findings highlight the need for further research and development of XME techniques to address these challenges. For more comprehensive information, the dataset used in this research and the associated code are publicly available at the following URL\url{https://github.com/lingo-iitgn/XME}.

papers.title: When classifying grammatical role, BERT doesn't care about word order...\n except when it matters
papers.research_question: How do BERT and GPT-2 represent grammatical role (subject vs. object), and is this representation sensitive to word order, especially in sentences where lexical semantics are insufficient?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that while early layer embeddings in BERT and GPT-2 are dominated by lexical semantics, word order becomes crucial in later layers for representing grammatical role in non-prototypical sentences, allowing models to override lexical cues.
papers.conclusion: Considering non-prototypical instances is crucial for understanding how language models represent language, as the combinatorial power of syntax is most evident when expressing surprising or impossible meanings.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantics dominates early layer representations, while grammatical information is gradually acquired in later layers for non-prototypical sentences.
Models learn to represent the effect of syntactic word order on meaning independently from distributional information, as shown by accurate classification on argument-swapped sentences.
General positional information (e.g., primacy) is insufficient for grammatical role classification in non-prototypical cases; fine-grained syntactic word order is necessary.
Probing on average (prototypical) sentences obscures the gradual acquisition of syntactic information, which is only visible when analyzing non-prototypical cases.
The ability to understand non-prototypical meanings, a hallmark of human language, is present in the models' later-layer representations.
papers.abstract:
Because meaning can often be inferred from lexical semantics alone, word
order is often a redundant cue in natural language. For example, the words
chopped, chef, and onion are more likely used to convey "The chef chopped the
onion," not "The onion chopped the chef." Recent work has shown large language
models to be surprisingly word order invariant, but crucially has largely
considered natural prototypical inputs, where compositional meaning mostly
matches lexical expectations. To overcome this confound, we probe grammatical
role representation in English BERT and GPT-2, on instances where lexical
expectations are not sufficient, and word order knowledge is necessary for
correct classification. Such non-prototypical instances are naturally occurring
English sentences with inanimate subjects or animate objects, or sentences
where we systematically swap the arguments to make sentences like "The onion
chopped the chef". We find that, while early layer embeddings are largely
lexical, word order is in fact crucial in defining the later-layer
representations of words in semantically non-prototypical positions. Our
experiments isolate the effect of word order on the contextualization process,
and highlight how models use context in the uncommon, but critical, instances
where it matters.

papers.title: Language Models as Models of Language
papers.research_question: What can modern language models contribute to theoretical linguistics, particularly regarding language acquisition and competence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models, when trained on developmentally plausible data and tested with controlled experiments, can serve as testbeds for evaluating linguistic hypotheses and inform debates about linguistic nativism.
papers.conclusion: Closer collaboration between theoretical linguists and computational researchers could yield valuable insights, particularly in advancing debates about linguistic nativism.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can learn hierarchical syntactic structure from exposure to data.
Language models exhibit sensitivity to various linguistic phenomena, even with developmentally plausible amounts of data.
Language models have inductive biases that favor natural language structures over impossible languages.
Language models can be used to test learnability claims and challenge strong nativist positions.
Causal intervention methods can help uncover the mechanisms by which language models process syntax.
papers.limitation: There is a large discrepancy between the amount of data used to train state-of-the-art language models and the data available to children during language acquisition.
future_direction: Using language models trained on developmentally plausible data (e.g., the BabyLM challenge).
Employing causal intervention methods to better understand model mechanisms.
Fostering closer collaboration between theoretical linguists and computational researchers.
papers.abstract: This chapter critically examines the potential contributions of modern language models to theoretical linguistics. Despite their focus on engineering goals, these models' ability to acquire sophisticated linguistic knowledge from mere exposure to data warrants a careful reassessment of their relevance to linguistic theory. I review a growing body of empirical evidence suggesting that language models can learn hierarchical syntactic structure and exhibit sensitivity to various linguistic phenomena, even when trained on developmentally plausible amounts of data. While the competence/performance distinction has been invoked to dismiss the relevance of such models to linguistic theory, I argue that this assessment may be premature. By carefully controlling learning conditions and making use of causal intervention methods, experiments with language models can potentially constrain hypotheses about language acquisition and competence. I conclude that closer collaboration between theoretical linguists and computational researchers could yield valuable insights, particularly in advancing debates about linguistic nativism.

papers.title: Understanding Syntax in Large Language Models: Successes and Limitations
papers.research_question: How accurately can LLMs handle published examples of complex syntactic phenomena, as described in linguistic theories?
papers.core_contribution: This study evaluates the syntactic competence of LLMs, finding that while they handle simple constructions well, they struggle with complex hierarchical dependencies, highlighting the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles.
papers.conclusion: LLMs demonstrate competence in simple syntax but struggle with complex structures, indicating a gap between surface fluency and deep syntactic competence, necessitating hybrid approaches for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit high success rates for simple relative clauses and basic wh-movement, but performance declines with increased complexity.
Center-embedding poses significant challenges, with success rates dropping to around 50% for deeply embedded structures.
Errors include truncation of sentences, unresolved syntactic dependencies, and semantic incoherence in complex cases.
LLMs rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than deep generative syntactic principles.
The limitations suggest that current LLMs lack robust internal representations of hierarchical syntax.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relied exclusively on examples from English linguistic literature, not capturing syntactic diversity across languages.
The evaluation focused only on relative clauses, wh-movement, and center-embedding, without exploring broader syntactic constructs.
The study was limited to publicly available LLMs like GPT-4 and BERT, without considering effects of model size, architecture, or training data.
The evaluation did not delve into underlying representations or mechanisms of the models.
future_direction: Integrating explicit syntactic theory into neural architectures, such as the Minimalist Program or dependency grammar.
Conducting cross-linguistic comparisons to evaluate LLMs' syntactic competence across different languages.
Designing more linguistically focused benchmarks based on theoretical constructs like syntactic islands or scope ambiguity.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to process complex syntactic phenomena, including relative clauses, wh-movement, and center- embedding. By analyzing examples derived from linguistic literature, the study highlights both the strengths and limitations of LLMs in handling syntax. The results reveal that while LLMs exhibit competence in simpler syntactic constructions, they struggle with deeper hierarchical dependencies and abstract syntactic constraints. The study underscores the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles into LLM architectures to bridge the gap between surface-level fluency and generative linguistic competence.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language\n Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind syntactic agreement in neural language models, specifically how do models prefer grammatical inflections and do neurons process agreement similarly across different syntactic structures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that language models use two distinct mechanisms for subject-verb agreement depending on whether the subject and verb are adjacent, and that larger models do not necessarily learn stronger preferences.
papers.conclusion: The study applies causal mediation analysis to reveal mechanisms behind syntactic agreement in pre-trained language models, showing how neurons are implicated and providing insights into model inner workings.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2 and Transformer-XL use two distinct mechanisms for subject-verb agreement: one for adjacent subject-verb pairs and another for non-adjacent pairs, while XLNet uses a unified mechanism.
Larger models have more distributed agreement mechanisms across layers, but do not always have stronger preferences for correct inflections.
The overlap of high-NIE neurons across syntactic structures correlates with human intuitions of syntactic similarity.
Plural subjects consistently have higher grammaticality values than singular subjects across structures.
Adverbial distractors increase the probability of correct verb inflections more than incorrect ones, while attractors decrease total effects.
future_direction: Intervening on groups of neurons and attention heads to see how components work together
Extending the analysis to phenomena such as filler-gap dependencies and negative polarity items
Examining the impact of specific verbs on syntactic agreement mechanisms
papers.abstract:
Targeted syntactic evaluations have demonstrated the ability of language
models to perform subject-verb agreement given difficult contexts. To elucidate
the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior, this study applies
causal mediation analysis to pre-trained neural language models. We investigate
the magnitude of models' preferences for grammatical inflections, as well as
whether neurons process subject-verb agreement similarly across sentences with
different syntactic structures. We uncover similarities and differences across
architectures and model sizes -- notably, that larger models do not necessarily
learn stronger preferences. We also observe two distinct mechanisms for
producing subject-verb agreement depending on the syntactic structure of the
input sentence. Finally, we find that language models rely on similar sets of
neurons when given sentences with similar syntactic structure.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects: Discrepancy between Performance and Competence
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between performance and competence in LLMs' linguistic understanding? How do LLMs represent form and meaning across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurolinguistic method (minimal pair probing) to assess LLMs' linguistic competence, revealing a distinction between performance and competence, and showing LLMs have stronger form competence than meaning competence.
papers.conclusion: This study adopts both psycho- and neuro-linguistic approaches to evaluating LLMs, revealing a distinction between linguistic performance and competence, and highlights the limitations of LLMs' semantic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct.
Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence.
Instruction tuning improves performance but does not significantly change competence.
LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning.
LLMs encode form earlier than meaning.
papers.limitation:
Limited range of languages covered in experiments.
Poor German evaluation results potentially due to very long sentences in the DistilLingEval dataset.
Experiments conducted on small-scale LLMs due to computational resource constraints.
COMPS dataset for conceptual understanding is not sufficiently fine-grained, limited to only four types of conceptual relationships.
future_direction: Include experiments covering a wider range of languages.
Construct syntactic minimal pair datasets for German.
Explore larger models to validate and extend generalizability.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the linguistic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) regarding signifier (form) and signified (meaning) by distinguishing two LLM assessment paradigms: psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic. Traditional psycholinguistic evaluations often reflect statistical rules that may not accurately represent LLMs' true linguistic competence. We introduce a neurolinguistic approach, utilizing a novel method that combines minimal pair and diagnostic probing to analyze activation patterns across model layers. This method allows for a detailed examination of how LLMs represent form and meaning, and whether these representations are consistent across languages. We found: (1) Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct; (2) Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence; (3) Instruction tuning won't change much competence but improve performance; (4) LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning. Additionally, we introduce new conceptual minimal pair datasets for Chinese (COMPS-ZH) and German (COMPS-DE), complementing existing English datasets.

papers.title: Multilingual Chart-based Constituency Parse Extraction from Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we extract constituency parses from pre-trained language models without training, and can this be done effectively across multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a chart-based method and a top-K ensemble technique for extracting constituency parses from pre-trained language models without training, and demonstrates that multilingual PLMs enable effective parsing across multiple languages.
papers.conclusion: The chart-based method and top-K ensemble improve constituency parse extraction from PLMs, and multilingual PLMs enable effective parsing across multiple languages, providing a foundation for unsupervised parsing for under-represented languages and probing multilingual PLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Chart-based methods (CP and CC) outperform the top-down method (TD) in most cases.
The top-K ensemble technique significantly improves parsing performance.
Multilingual PLMs can be used for constituency parse extraction across multiple languages, achieving performance comparable or superior to unsupervised PCFGs.
The method is robust to cross-lingual transfer, with minimal performance loss when using attention heads selected for English on other languages.
There exist universal attention heads that are sensitive to syntactic information across languages.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on a validation set for hyperparameter selection (attention head selection), so it is not entirely unsupervised.
The performance, while competitive, still falls short of standard supervised parsers.
The chart parsing algorithm has O(n^3) time complexity, which is less efficient than top-down parsing.
future_direction: Developing a method that is free from validation set annotations.
Designing an ensemble method that gathers information from heterogeneous PLMs.
Thorough analysis of the effect of parsing strategies across languages.
papers.abstract: As it has been unveiled that pre-trained language models (PLMs) are to some extent capable of recognizing syntactic concepts in natural language, much effort has been made to develop a method for extracting complete (binary) parses from PLMs without training separate parsers. We improve upon this paradigm by proposing a novel chart-based method and an effective top-K ensemble technique. Moreover, we demonstrate that we can broaden the scope of application of the approach into multilingual settings. Specifically, we show that by applying our method on multilingual PLMs, it becomes possible to induce non-trivial parses for sentences from nine languages in an integrated and language-agnostic manner, attaining performance superior or comparable to that of unsupervised PCFGs. We also verify that our approach is robust to cross-lingual transfer. Finally, we provide analyses on the inner workings of our method. For instance, we discover universal attention heads which are consistently sensitive to syntactic information irrespective of the input language.

papers.title: Joint processing of linguistic properties in brains and language models
papers.research_question: What linguistic properties are responsible for the alignment between brain recordings (fMRI) and language model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a direct approach to evaluate joint linguistic processing in brains and language models by removing specific linguistic properties from model representations, showing this significantly decreases brain alignment, with syntactic properties having the largest effect.
papers.conclusion: The direct approach provides clear evidence that specific linguistic information, particularly syntactic properties, underlies the alignment between brain and language models, opening new avenues for mapping joint information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Removing each tested linguistic property (surface, syntactic, semantic) results in a significant decrease in brain alignment across all layers of BERT and GPT-2.
Syntactic properties (Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the largest effect on the trend of brain alignment across model layers.
Top Constituents affects alignment in all language brain regions, while Tree Depth specifically affects temporal (ATL, PTL) and frontal (IFG, MFG) regions.
Semantic properties (Tense, Subject Number, Object Number) affect alignment more specifically in regions like the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC).
The method reveals that different linguistic properties are important for alignment in different brain regions and sub-regions.
papers.limitation:
The removal approach may also remove information correlated with the removed linguistic property due to dataset limitations.
Substantial brain alignment remains after removing all tested properties, indicating not all relevant linguistic properties have been accounted for.
The study is limited to English language stimuli and two language models (BERT and GPT-2).
future_direction: Incorporate additional linguistic properties to fully characterize joint processing.
Investigate larger language models beyond BERT and GPT-2.
Extend the approach to languages beyond English.
papers.abstract: Language models have been shown to be very effective in predicting brain recordings of subjects experiencing complex language stimuli. For a deeper understanding of this alignment, it is important to understand the correspondence between the detailed processing of linguistic information by the human brain versus language models. We investigate this correspondence via a direct approach, in which we eliminate information related to specific linguistic properties in the language model representations and observe how this intervention affects the alignment with fMRI brain recordings obtained while participants listened to a story. We investigate a range of linguistic properties (surface, syntactic, and semantic) and find that the elimination of each one results in a significant decrease in brain alignment. Specifically, we find that syntactic properties (i.e. Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the largest effect on the trend of brain alignment across model layers. These findings provide clear evidence for the role of specific linguistic information in the alignment between brain and language models, and open new avenues for mapping the joint information processing in both systems. We make the code publicly available [https://github.com/subbareddy248/linguistic-properties-brain-alignment].

papers.title: Attention weights accurately predict language representations in the brain
papers.research_question: Are attention weights in Transformer-based language models related to language representations in the brain? Can attention weights predict brain responses to language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights from Transformer-based language models accurately predict brain responses in language-related cortical areas, and contain information not captured by lexical or contextual embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Attention weights in Transformer-based LMs capture information that is reflected in brain representations during language processing, and indicate cortical areas that could be involved in integrating context across words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 accurately predict brain responses in frontal and temporal cortices associated with language processing.
Attention weights better predict brain responses than lexical embeddings in many language-related areas.
Attention weights from middle layers of BERT explain the most variance in brain responses, consistent with linguistic relevance of middle layers.
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 perform similarly in predicting brain responses, suggesting consistency across unidirectional and bidirectional models.
In some cortical areas, attention weights predict brain responses better than contextual embeddings, indicating additional information in attention weights.
papers.limitation:
The temporal resolution of fMRI (2s) does not capture all the rapid changes in human speech.
Analyses were limited to English language comprehension.
The analyses demonstrate similarity of representations between Transformer-based LMs and brain responses, but do not directly prove the existence of similar underlying computational mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other languages to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of context integration in the brain and in artificial neural networks.

Compare the results of our method of computing attention weights with more cognitively-inspired methods to provide more specific insights into how attention weights in Transformer-based LMs relate to processes in the human brain.
papers.abstract: In Transformer-based language models (LMs) the attention mechanism converts token embeddings into contextual embeddings that incorporate information from neighboring words. The resulting contextual hidden state embeddings have enabled highly accurate models of brain responses, suggesting that the attention mechanism constructs contextual embeddings that carry information reflected in language-related brain representations. However, it is unclear whether the attention weights that are used to integrate information across words are themselves related to language representations in the brain. To address this question we analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings of participants reading English language narratives. We provided the narrative text as input to two LMs (BERT and GPT-2) and extracted their corresponding attention weights. We then used encoding models to determine how well attention weights can predict recorded brain responses. We find that attention weights accurately predict brain responses in much of the frontal and temporal cortices. Our results suggest that the attention mechanism itself carries information that is reflected in brain representations. Moreover, these results indicate cortical areas in which context integration may occur.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of\n Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the stacked layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interventional, input perturbation-based analysis method to show that Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, with larger contexts and more complex phrase boundaries becoming more salient in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process; structured input perturbations are a useful tool for analyzing deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing characteristic scale of context along layers.
Swapping two constituent phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrase spans of the same length, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, indicating sensitivity to phrase hierarchy.
Changes in attention weights partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance, with deeper layers showing more correlation.
The observed sensitivities are not due to simple co-occurrence statistics, as shown by controlling for PMI.
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features
Searching for the causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance
Exploring applications in network pruning studies
Extending the method as a hypothesis generator in neuroscience to understand compositional structure in neural populations
papers.abstract:
While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models
have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete
accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear
what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations,
nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In
this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of
interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from
pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive
neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of
probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several
kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a
sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the
original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random
permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a
representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which
do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase
structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break
apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure.
 Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build
sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that
hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our
results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of
analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can
serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for
interpreting complex black-box models.

papers.title: Linguistically Grounded Analysis of Language Models using Shapley Head Values
papers.research_question: How is linguistic knowledge, specifically morphosyntactic phenomena, encoded and processed in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Shapley Head Values (SHVs) can identify attention heads that form subnetworks corresponding to linguistic phenomena, and that pruning these heads affects model performance on related grammaticality judgment tasks.
papers.conclusion: SHV-based attributions can identify attention heads of subnetworks that generalize across related morphosyntactic phenomena, enabling linguistically grounded analysis of how language models organize linguistic information.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads responsible for processing related linguistic phenomena cluster together based on SHV attributions.
SHV-based clustering reveals consistent patterns across BERT and RoBERTa for 6 out of 10 clusters.
Pruning the top attention heads identified by SHVs significantly impacts accuracy for in-cluster paradigms, indicating localized processing of linguistic knowledge.
RoBERTa shows more discerning clustering than BERT, possibly due to more training data and parameters.
The methodology supports the hypothesis that language models learn internal subnetworks corresponding to theoretical linguistic categories.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty scaling to new languages and models due to lack of datasets and need for manual linguistic analysis.
BLiMP sentences are semantically empty and formulaic, though this is not likely to cause problems for attributions.
SHV derivation uses sampling and truncation heuristics, introducing uncertainty in the attribution process.
Binary gates for zeroing attention heads may harm model performance because zero-values are out-of-distribution.
Attributions are at the attention head level, not neuron level, which may lose granularity.
future_direction: Cross-lingual application of the method to analyze subnetworks in other languages.
papers.abstract: Understanding how linguistic knowledge is encoded in language models is crucial for improving their generalisation capabilities.In this paper, we investigate the processing of morphosyntactic phenomena, by leveraging a recently proposed method for probing language models via Shapley Head Values (SHVs).Using the English language BLiMP dataset, we test our approach on two widely used models, BERT and RoBERTa, and compare how linguistic constructions such as anaphor agreement and filler-gap dependencies are handled.Through quantitative pruning and qualitative clustering analysis, we demonstrate that attention heads responsible for processing related linguistic phenomena cluster together.Our results show that SHV-based attributions reveal distinct patterns across both models, providing insights into how language models organize and process linguistic information.These findings support the hypothesis that language models learn subnetworks corresponding to linguistic theory, with potential implications for crosslinguistic model analysis and interpretability in natural language processing (NLP).Phenomenon N Acceptable Example Unacceptable Example ANAPHOR AGR. 2 Many girls insulted themselves.*Many girls insulted herself.ARG.STRUCTURE 7 Rose wasn't disturbing Mark.*Rose wasn't boasting Mark.BINDING THEORY 7 Carlos said that Lori helped him.*Carlos said that Lori helped himself.CONTROL/RAISING 5 There was bound to be a fish escaping.*There was unable to be a fish escaping

papers.title: Beyond English-Centric LLMs: What Language Do Multilingual Language Models Think in?
papers.research_question: What internal latent language do non-English-centric large language models use in their intermediate layers when processing tasks?
papers.core_contribution: This study demonstrates that the internal latent language of LLMs is determined by their training corpora, with Japanese-specific models using Japanese as a latent language. For non-dominant target languages, models activate the latent language most closely related to it, and the transition from latent to target language occurs in sparse dimensions related to language identity.
papers.conclusion: The internal latent language of LLMs is majorly determined by the language of its training corpora. The transition from latent to target language involves sparse dimensions related to language identity, providing insights for understanding model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Japanese-specific models (Swallow, LLM-jp) use Japanese as an internal latent language when processing Japanese, unlike English-centric Llama-2.
When processing non-dominant languages (French, Chinese), Swallow and LLM-jp exhibit dual internal latent languages (English and Japanese), preferring the one more closely related to the target language.
In culture-conflict QA tasks, intermediate layers initially produce answers biased by the culture of the internal latent language before aligning with the target language context.
The shift from internal latent language to target language representation occurs only in sparse dimensions of the hidden vectors, which are inferred to be related to language identity.
papers.limitation: An exception in Swallow's translation results (higher Japanese probability for French target than Chinese) may be due to specific content in its training corpus, but this hypothesis is difficult to verify.
future_direction: Extend investigation to models with other specific dominant languages, such as Chinese, French, and Arabic.
papers.abstract: In this study, we investigate whether non-English-centric LLMs, despite their strong performance, `think' in their respective dominant language: more precisely, `think' refers to how the representations of intermediate layers, when un-embedded into the vocabulary space, exhibit higher probabilities for certain dominant languages during generation. We term such languages as internal $\textbf{latent languages}$. We examine the latent language of three typical categories of models for Japanese processing: Llama2, an English-centric model; Swallow, an English-centric model with continued pre-training in Japanese; and LLM-jp, a model pre-trained on balanced English and Japanese corpora. Our empirical findings reveal that, unlike Llama2 which relies exclusively on English as the internal latent language, Japanese-specific Swallow and LLM-jp employ both Japanese and English, exhibiting dual internal latent languages. For any given target language, the model preferentially activates the latent language most closely related to it. In addition, we explore how intermediate layers respond to questions involving cultural conflicts between latent internal and target output languages. We further explore how the language identity shifts across layers while keeping consistent semantic meaning reflected in the intermediate layer representations. This study deepens the understanding of non-English-centric large language models, highlighting the intricate dynamics of language representation within their intermediate layers.

papers.title: Incremental Processing of Principle B: Mismatches Between Neural Models and Humans
papers.research_question: Do GPT-based autoregressive neural language models use Principle B to restrict their incremental coreference processing like humans? Specifically, does Principle B block the influence of ungrammatical structural positions on pronoun prediction and cataphoric processing?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-based language models do not categorically ignore structural positions blocked by Principle B during incremental coreference processing, unlike humans. This mismatch suggests that certain aspects of human parsing behavior are not directly evidenced in linguistic data and may relate to properties of the training data.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive neural models do not uniformly process pronouns like humans; they fail to capture qualitative patterns of incremental coreference processing and underestimate processing costs. Models appear to learn only those aspects of Principle B that have predictable reflexes in training data.
papers.key_findings:
For object pronouns (him) in positions where Principle B blocks co-indexation, all models exhibited a negative Gender Mismatch Effect (GMME), meaning they expected the pronoun to mismatch in gender with the grammatically unavailable antecedent.
For possessive pronouns (his), all models showed positive GMMEs across all structural positions, expecting gender agreement with antecedents.
In cataphoric object pronoun processing, larger models (GPT-J and GPT-3) showed no significant GMME when Principle B blocked coreference, aligning with human behavior, while smaller models (GPT-2 XL and GPT-Neo) showed a positive GMME.
Neural models greatly underestimate the magnitude of processing costs observed in humans, even in cases of qualitative overlap.
Analysis of the training data (the Pile) reveals a surface distribution bias where pronouns are more likely to mismatch in gender with antecedents in positions blocked by Principle B, suggesting models may overfit this pattern.
papers.limitation:
Whether models truly 'interpret' the correct coreference relations is unclear; techniques are limited for assessing if models comprehend meaning in a human-like fashion.
The study relies on stereotypical associations between nouns and pronouns, which does not cleanly map onto the real world (e.g., singular they is not considered).
The investigation is limited to English, due to resource availability and the focus of existing psycholinguistic work, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Future work might consider analyses of the attention mechanisms to dig deeper into what information models are using.
papers.abstract: Despite neural language models qualitatively capturing many human linguistic behaviors, recent work has demonstrated that they underestimate the true processing costs of ungrammatical structures. We extend these more fine-grained comparisons between humans and models by investigating the interaction between Principle B and coreference processing. While humans use Principle B to block certain structural positions from affecting their incremental processing, we find that GPT-based language models are influenced by ungrammatical positions. We conclude by relating the mismatch between neural models and humans to properties of training data and suggest that certain aspects of human processing behavior do not directly follow from linguistic data.Paper at CoNLL 2022

papers.title: Language Models as Artificial Learners: Investigating Crosslinguistic Influence
papers.research_question: How do L1 dominance and L2 proficiency affect crosslinguistic influence in language models, and can LMs serve as a computational framework to study human CLI?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language models can simulate crosslinguistic influence, showing that L1 dominance and L2 proficiency predict CLI, and provides mechanistic evidence of L1 co-activation during L2 processing.
papers.conclusion: LMs can serve as artificial learners to study CLI, and the findings suggest a hybrid account where shared structures are bidirectionally primed, while non-overlapping structures are separate-but-connected and influenced by dominance.
papers.key_findings:
CLI effects are modulated by syntactic distance: similar L1 languages cause less interference or more facilitation.
Crosslinguistic priming is bidirectional for grammatical structures but sensitive to language dominance for ungrammatical structures.
LMs show preference for non-native constructions from the same L1, especially after priming.
LogitLens shows L1 token presence during L2 processing increases with L1 dominance.
L2 neuron overlap between L1 languages correlates negatively with syntactic distance.
papers.abstract: Despite the centrality of crosslinguistic influence (CLI) to bilingualism research, human studies often yield conflicting results due to inherent experimental variance. We address these inconsistencies by using language models (LMs) as controlled statistical learners to systematically simulate CLI and isolate its underlying drivers. Specifically, we study the effect of varying the L1 language dominance and the L2 language proficiency, which we manipulate by controlling the L2 age of exposure -- defined as the training step at which the L2 is introduced. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of pretraining on L1 languages with varying syntactic distance from the L2. Using cross-linguistic priming, we analyze how activating L1 structures impacts L2 processing. Our results align with evidence from psycholinguistic studies, confirming that language dominance and proficiency are strong predictors of CLI. We further find that while priming of grammatical structures is bidirectional, the priming of ungrammatical structures is sensitive to language dominance. Finally, we provide mechanistic evidence of CLI in LMs, demonstrating that the L1 is co-activated during L2 processing and directly influences the neural circuitry recruited for the L2. More broadly, our work demonstrates that LMs can serve as a computational framework to inform theories of human CLI.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers: A cross-lingual exploration of knowledge
papers.research_question: This study examines the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and investigates the role of attention mechanisms in this process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes MEMAT, a knowledge editing method that modifies attention heads in addition to MLP layers, leading to improved performance, cross-lingual portability, and enhanced model understanding of edited facts.
papers.conclusion: MEMAT improves knowledge editing by leveraging attention heads, demonstrating portability and effectiveness across languages, and enhancing the model's understanding of the inserted factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT's cross-lingual performance is dependent on subject tokenization similarity between languages.
Attention heads encode language-independent information about factual associations, achieving high accuracy in classifying truthful sentences.
MEMAT outperforms MEMIT across all evaluation metrics (success and magnitude), with improvements exceeding 10% in some cases.
The attention head corrections learned by MEMAT are portable and can be recycled for editing new sets of factual triplets.
MEMAT enhances the model's comprehension of the edited knowledge rather than merely reintroducing it, as evidenced by improved paraphrase and neighborhood metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to English and Catalan; generalization to other linguistic contexts may be limited due to alphabet similarity.
Broader challenges in knowledge editing persist, such as the inability to modify related knowledge and lack of bidirectionality.
future_direction: Investigating language adaptation techniques to enable models to perform tasks in a more language-agnostic manner.
Exploring the role that each architecture component plays in alternative domains to enhance explainable AI.
papers.abstract: Recent research has explored methods for updating and modifying factual knowledge in large language models, often focusing on specific multi-layer perceptron blocks. This study expands on this work by examining the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and delving into the role of attention mechanisms in this process. Drawing from the insights gained, we propose Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers (MEMAT), a method that achieves significant improvements in all metrics while requiring minimal parameter modifications. MEMAT delivers a remarkable 10% increase in magnitude metrics, benefits languages not included in the training data and also demonstrates a high degree of portability. Our code and data are at https://github.com/dtamayo-nlp/MEMAT.

papers.title: Exploring Multilingual Probing in Large Language Models: A Cross-Language Analysis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether other languages achieve comparable probing accuracy to English, whether they exhibit similar layer-wise behavioral patterns to English, and what the similarities are between probing vectors across different languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends probing techniques to a multilingual context and reveals significant disparities in LLMs' performance and representational qualities between high-resource and low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and suggest that these models may not be learning deeper linguistic concepts effectively across all languages, especially low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
High-resource languages achieve higher probing accuracy than low-resource languages.
High-resource languages exhibit similar layer-wise trends to English, with accuracy improving in deeper layers, while low-resource languages show stable or only slight improvement.
Probing vectors of high-resource languages are more similar to each other, while low-resource languages have lower similarities among themselves and with high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Using machine translation to generate prompts and questions may introduce noise.
Only five open-source LLMs and two datasets are experimented with, limiting generalizability.
Only linear classifier probing is used; more sophisticated probing methods could offer deeper insights.
future_direction: Develop more equitable and effective multilingual language models that can better capture universal linguistic concepts.
Extend the research to multimodal models that incorporate visual and textual information.
Explore more sophisticated probing methods beyond linear classifiers.
papers.abstract: Probing techniques for large language models (LLMs) have primarily focused on English, overlooking the vast majority of the world's languages. In this paper, we extend these probing methods to a multilingual context, investigating the behaviors of LLMs across diverse languages. We conduct experiments on several open-source LLM models, analyzing probing accuracy, trends across layers, and similarities between probing vectors for multiple languages. Our key findings reveal: (1) a consistent performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages, with high-resource languages achieving significantly higher probing accuracy; (2) divergent layer-wise accuracy trends, where high-resource languages show substantial improvement in deeper layers similar to English; and (3) higher representational similarities among high-resource languages, with low-resource languages demonstrating lower similarities both among themselves and with high-resource languages. These results highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and emphasize the need for improved modeling of low-resource languages.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Discourse structure interacts with reference but not syntax in neural\n language models
papers.research_question: Does discourse structure (implicit causality) influence reference and syntactic processing in neural language models, and how does this compare to human behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models learn a representational distinction for implicit causality that influences reference resolution but not syntactic attachment, while LSTM language models fail to learn such a distinction, revealing a mismatch between learned representations and behavior in language models.
papers.conclusion: Language models can learn discourse structure (implicit causality) from text, but they do not consistently use this knowledge in behavior, especially for syntactic processing, indicating limitations in how they acquire and utilize linguistic abstractions.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM language models show no influence of implicit causality on reference or syntax.
TransformerXL shows partial implicit causality representation, influencing reference but not syntax.
GPT-2 XL shows robust implicit causality effects on reference, matching human behavior, but not on syntax.
Transformers encode implicit causality in representations for both reference and syntax, but this knowledge does not affect syntactic behavior.
Both transformer models show a strong preference for local agreement in syntax, overriding discourse effects.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to unidirectional models and specific architectures, so mechanistic claims about the relationship between learned linguistic knowledge and model configurations are cautioned.
The representational similarity measure (Pearson's r) may not be optimal for capturing the relevant distinctions, especially for LSTM models.
The models may be unable to learn the syntactic operation of attachment, as suggested by the erasure of number agreement in final layers.
future_direction: Investigate the role of training objectives, such as predicting coherence relations instead of next-word prediction.
Explore the exact role of training data and model architecture in learning linguistic interactions.
Cross-linguistic studies to further understand the limitations of language models in learning syntax.
papers.abstract:
Language models (LMs) trained on large quantities of text have been claimed
to acquire abstract linguistic representations. Our work tests the robustness
of these abstractions by focusing on the ability of LMs to learn interactions
between different linguistic representations. In particular, we utilized
stimuli from psycholinguistic studies showing that humans can condition
reference (i.e. coreference resolution) and syntactic processing on the same
discourse structure (implicit causality). We compared both transformer and long
short-term memory LMs to find that, contrary to humans, implicit causality only
influences LM behavior for reference, not syntax, despite model representations
that encode the necessary discourse information. Our results further suggest
that LM behavior can contradict not only learned representations of discourse
but also syntactic agreement, pointing to shortcomings of standard language
modeling.

papers.title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models using Minimal Pairs
papers.research_question: How do neural language models capture linguistic information internally, specifically using minimal pairs to probe grammaticality across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel 'decoding probing' method inspired by cognitive neuroscience to reveal internal linguistic structures in neural language models using minimal pairs, demonstrating that self-supervised models capture abstract linguistic features in intermediate layers with distinct patterns for syntax, morphology, and semantics.
papers.conclusion: Decoding probing bridges cognitive neuroscience and NLP, providing insights into hierarchical linguistic feature capture in LMs, with semantics-syntax interface and morphology being more challenging than syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn.
Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and distributed in later layers; more layers are required for complex sentences.
Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax.
For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns, with attention heads exhibiting similar tendencies but varied contributions.
papers.limitation: Focuses mainly on structure grammaticality with limited attention to conceptual capabilities.
future_direction: Apply decoding probe methods to reveal LM's ability to master concepts using the COMPS minimal pair dataset.
papers.abstract: Inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies, we introduce a novel `decoding probing' method that uses minimal pairs benchmark (BLiMP) to probe internal linguistic characteristics in neural language models layer by layer. By treating the language model as the `brain' and its representations as `neural activations', we decode grammaticality labels of minimal pairs from the intermediate layers' representations. This approach reveals: 1) Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn. 2) Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and also distributed in later layers. As sentence complexity increases, more layers are required for learning grammatical capabilities. 3) Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax. 4) For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns. Different attention heads exhibit similar tendencies toward various linguistic phenomena, but with varied contributions.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: The Grammar of Transformers: A Systematic Review of Interpretability Research on Syntactic Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What do Transformer-based language models (TLMs) learn about syntax from the language modeling task?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic review of 337 articles on syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models, identifying an over-focus on English and BERT, and finding that TLMs capture form-oriented syntactic phenomena well but perform more variably on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface.
papers.conclusion: The review reveals a rich but heterogeneous landscape in syntactic interpretability research, with tentative evidence that formal syntax is easier for models than the syntax-semantics interface, and highlights the need for broader empirical scope and better data reporting.
papers.key_findings:
There is an over-focus on a single language (English) and a single model (BERT) in the literature.
TLMs perform better on formal syntactic phenomena (e.g., agreement) than on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface (e.g., binding).
The field uses a balanced variety of interpretability methods (behavioral, mechanistic, probing), but probing has declined in recent years.
Multilingual and typological aspects of syntax are underexplored.
BLiMP benchmark scores show that model performance scales with training data size and that bidirectional models tend to outperform causal models for given data sizes.
future_direction: Reporting complete data in studies.
Better aligning theoretical constructs and methods across studies.
Increasing the use of mechanistic methods.
Broadening the empirical scope regarding languages and linguistic phenomena.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic review of 337 articles evaluating the syntactic abilities of Transformer-based language models, reporting on 1,015 model results from a range of syntactic phenomena and interpretability methods. Our analysis shows that the state of the art presents a healthy variety of methods and data, but an over-focus on a single language (English), a single model (BERT), and phenomena that are easy to get at (like part of speech and agreement). Results also suggest that TLMs capture these form-oriented phenomena well, but show more variable and weaker performance on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface, like binding or filler-gap dependencies. We provide recommendations for future work, in particular reporting complete data, better aligning theoretical constructs and methods across studies, increasing the use of mechanistic methods, and broadening the empirical scope regarding languages and linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: Unveiling Visual Perception in Language Models: An Attention Head Analysis Approach
papers.research_question: How can language models, initially trained solely on linguistic data, effectively interpret and process visual content? Specifically, what is the attention mechanism doing when processing visual tokens?
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies a unique class of attention heads in Multimodal Large Language Models that specialize in processing visual tokens. These 'visual heads' are concentrated in specific layers (primarily early and middle) and their behavior, characterized by attention weight and concentration, is critical for visual understanding and correlates with model performance.
papers.conclusion: Visual heads in LLMs are concentrated in specific layers, primarily early and middle stages, and play a key role in processing visual tokens. Early-stage heads are critical for visual understanding, while late-stage heads contribute minimally, offering potential for pruning to improve computational efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Visual heads are concentrated in specific layers, primarily early and middle stages, unlike retrieval heads which are more universally distributed.
Visual heads exhibit dynamic activation based on context, adjusting their function in response to varying visual and linguistic inputs.
High concentration of attention (sharp focus on specific image regions) correlates with better model performance on visual tasks.
Early-stage visual heads are critical for visual understanding; removing them leads to significant performance drops, while late-stage heads can be pruned with minimal impact, suggesting potential for efficient inference.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show enhanced consistency and adaptability of visual head behavior across diverse datasets.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in visual understanding. This impressive leap raises a compelling question: how can language models, initially trained solely on linguistic data, effectively interpret and process visual content? This paper aims to address this question with systematic investigation across 4 model families and 4 model scales, uncovering a unique class of attention heads that focus specifically on visual content. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between the behavior of these attention heads, the distribution of attention weights, and their concentration on visual tokens within the input. These findings enhance our understanding of how LLMs adapt to multimodal tasks, demonstrating their potential to bridge the gap between textual and visual understanding. This work paves the way for the development of AI systems capable of engaging with diverse modalities.

papers.title: Language Representation Projection: Can We Transfer Factual Knowledge across Languages in Multilingual Language Models?
papers.research_question: Can cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enable factual knowledge transfer across languages? Specifically, can we transfer factual knowledge from English to non-English languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes LRP2, a parameter-free method that projects representations between languages to align representation spaces, which improves factual knowledge retrieval and transfer across languages in multilingual language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper confirms that cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enables factual knowledge transfer across languages, and proposes LRP2 as an effective method for this transfer.
papers.key_findings:
LRP2 improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and cross-lingual transferability for non-English languages.
LRP2 aligns representation spaces: LIRP projects non-English representations to English-like ones, and LSRP projects them back to the non-English space.
LRP2 increases the overlap of knowledge neurons between English and non-English languages, indicating enhanced cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
Cross-lingual knowledge neurons exist in multilingual pretrained language models.
Different languages require different optimal layer configurations for the LIRP and LSRP modules, indicating varying degrees of representation alignment needed.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of LRP2 heavily relies on the inherent capabilities of multilingual pretrained language models.
Experiments are limited to two relatively small models due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Investigate LRP2 on larger language models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models serve as repositories of multilingual factual knowledge. Nevertheless, a substantial performance gap of factual knowledge probing exists between high-resource languages and low-resource languages, suggesting limited implicit factual knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual pretrained language models. This paper investigates the feasibility of explicitly transferring relatively rich factual knowledge from English to non-English languages. To accomplish this, we propose two parameter-free Language Representation Projection modules (LRP2). The first module converts non-English representations into English-like equivalents, while the second module reverts English-like representations back into representations of the corresponding non-English language. Experimental results on the mLAMA dataset demonstrate that LRP2 significantly improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and facilitates knowledge transferability across diverse non-English languages. We further investigate the working mechanism of LRP2 from the perspectives of representation space and cross-lingual knowledge neuron.

papers.title: Mechanisms vs. Outcomes: Probing for Syntax Fails to Explain Performance on Targeted Syntactic Evaluations
papers.research_question: Do probing accuracies, measured by dependency tree attachment scores of syntactic probes, effectively predict a model’s downstream performance on targeted syntactic evaluations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic features extracted via probing fail to predict outcomes of targeted syntax evaluations, highlighting a disconnect between latent syntactic representations and observable syntactic behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Probing fails to reliably extract the latent syntactic knowledge within models that correlates with minimal pair accuracy, arguing for targeted evaluations like BLiMP as the gold standard for assessing syntactic competence.
papers.key_findings:
No significant regression fit between probing accuracy and overall BLiMP minimal pair accuracy across 32 models.
Only anaphor agreement shows a significant correlation, but a non-syntactic control probe yields a similar fit, suggesting it is spurious.
Probe recovery of critical syntactic edges (e.g., subject-verb) only weakly aligns with minimal pair outcomes (40–60% match rate).
In over 85% of BLiMP paradigms, UUAS score distributions for correct and incorrect minimal pairs substantially overlap.
Control probes trained on non-syntactic information can also predict some syntactic benchmark performance, indicating that probing results may not be attributable solely to syntactic representations.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation only uses English grammatical benchmarks.
Probe architectures are limited to linear and bilinear probes; other architectures could yield different results.
Models are limited to up to 8B parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Extending the work to multilingual benchmarks (e.g., MultiBLiMP, TurBLiMP).
Exploring other probe architectures and syntactic probing tasks.
Investigating causal relationships between probed representations and model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a robust mastery of syntax when processing and generating text. While this suggests internalized understanding of hierarchical syntax and dependency relations, the precise mechanism by which they represent syntactic structure is an open area within interpretability research. Probing provides one way to identify the mechanism of syntax being linearly encoded in activations, however, no comprehensive study has yet established whether a model's probing accuracy reliably predicts its downstream syntactic performance. Adopting a "mechanisms vs. outcomes" framework, we evaluate 32 open-weight transformer models and find that syntactic features extracted via probing fail to predict outcomes of targeted syntax evaluations across English linguistic phenomena. Our results highlight a substantial disconnect between latent syntactic representations found via probing and observable syntactic behaviors in downstream tasks.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Partially Primed in Pronoun Interpretation
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) adapt their referential biases in pronoun interpretation in a human-like way when exposed to consistent referential patterns in the local discourse context?
papers.core_contribution: InstructGPT can adapt its syntactic bias in pronoun interpretation from exposure to referential patterns in the local context, but fails to adapt its semantic bias, suggesting LLMs only partially represent semantic knowledge in referential processing.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can adapt to syntactic patterns in pronoun interpretation from local exposure, but not to semantic patterns, indicating a partial and non-human-like representation of semantic knowledge in referential processing.
papers.key_findings:
InstructGPT adapted its syntactic bias (subject vs. non-subject preference) based on recent exposure, showing sensitivity to syntactic patterns in the local discourse.
InstructGPT exhibited a strong, persistent goal bias in pronoun interpretation that was not influenced by exposure to source/goal patterns, unlike human participants.
FLAN-UL2 failed to generate meaningful patterns, answering 'yes' 100% of the time to ambiguous target questions and showing poor comprehension.
The adaptation to syntactic patterns was observed even in the presence of confounding semantic goal bias (Experiment 2a).
